speechtext:
That this House condemn the Government for its destructive influence on the Canadian transportation industry by its impractical and slavish adherence to the ideological myth of deregulation and its inept trade negotiations with the United States, in particular, through:
(1)	deregulation of the trucking industry, giving U.S. truckers open access to Canadian markets while 43 heavily regulated American states deny Canadian truckers the same advantage;
(2)	introduction in the railway industry of "Competitive Rail Line Rate" provisions allowing American railways free access to Canadian markets while denying reciprocal arrangements for Canadian railways;
(3)	failing to seek and obtain in the trade agreement equitable treatment in the United States for Canadian airlines; and
(4)	abandoning its legislation on the Canadian coasting trade and failing to obtain any benefits in the trade agreement for Canadian maritime industries.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was concluded at the beginning of October, not many people wondered about the impact it would have on Canada's transportation industry. It is clear, however, that as far as transportation is concerned, Canada loses across the board. In fact, we have given our trucking industry away to the Americans through our massive deregulation in this country. The competitive line rates mechanism in Bill C-18 on deregulation of the transportation industry in Canada gives U.S. railway companies broad access to the Canadian market.
Furthermore, the air transportation industry, where we could have negotiated certain cabotage rights, has been excluded outright from the Free Trade Agreement. And lastly, after making so many concessions in the other sectors, we were turned down flatly when it came to shipping.
In fact, our marine industries are getting strictly nothing out of the free trade talks. As far as we of the Liberal Party of Canada are concerned, the transportation sector is losing
across the board. That is why today, we tabled this motion condemning the Conservative Government.
First, I would like to talk about marine transportation. This is what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) had to say in an interview with the Canadian press a few days ago.

He said he's disappointed that the terms of the transportation annex
attached to the free-trade agreement don't go far enough in freeing
transportation services from protective controls.
Do I have to remind Hon. Members that the Conservative Government's stated motive for entering into this treaty was, after all, to buy exemptions from protectionist U.S. law, an objective that has not been achieved at all?

By reserving the right to review the provisions on marine shipping in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, the U.S. Senate caught the Canadian Minister of Transport with his pants down. On September 23, the U.S. Senate Rules Committee approved a decision to amend the fast track formula that allowed the U.S. Senate to either accept or reject, but not amend, the Agreement. The U.S. Senate will now be allowed to amend the Agreement's provisions on marine shipping, but only those provisions. Now that fifty-six U.S. Senators and 253 members of Congress have signed resolutions asking that any provisions liable to harm U.S. merchant shipping be taken out of the Canada-U.S. Agreement, it seems their goal is to persuade the U.S. Administration to remove all provisions concerning coastal trade if it wants the rest of the Agreement to stand.
Judging by the second draft of the annex received last week, the Reagan Administration is taking this measure very seriously. It is therefore unfortunate that our Minister of Transport had to admit last Friday that he could do nothing. In fact, the latest document on the transportation industry has revealed that Canadian carriers will be excluded from any new marine shipping program, such as supplies for the U.S. Government and preferential commodities.
The Canadian marine industry had decided to challenge the Jones Act of 1920, the merchant marine legislation which regulates practically every aspect of the marine industry in the United States. The Canadian shipping companies were quite disappointed when they realized that the Free Trade Agreement would not result, as they had hoped, in the drawing-up of a "Jones Act" for the whole North American continent which, according to Mr. Fred Pitre, Vice President of the Canada Steamship Lines, would have combined the openness and

November 27, 1987

flexibility of the Canada Shipping Act with the national security guarantees of the Jones Act.
Speaking on behalf of the Dominion Marine Association, its president, Mr, Norman Hall, would want, in the absence of a global shipping free trade deal, the Canadian negotiators to at least consider the issue of discriminatory investment practices in the United States. An American marine company may now invest up to 100 per cent in a Canadian company and use a foreign built ship to transport goods from one Canadian port to another. On the other hand, a Canadian investor may purchase only 25 per cent of an American shipping firm and must use only ships built in the United States. The competition, therefore, is not fair and is totally disadvantageous to the Canadian economy. That is a blatant disparity which will be confirmed by the Reagan-Mulroney Agreement.
On the other hand, it would be to the advantage of Canadian shipyards and their employees that the Canadian coasting trade be protected just as the American merchant marine is under the Jones Act. Mr. Clarke, President of the Shipyards Association, for fear that a relaxation of the protective provisions would open Canada's door to ships built abroad, wishes to see the Canadian legislation provide the same protection as its American counterpart. Finally, the Seafarers International Union and the Merchant Service Guild, unions which represent some 5,000 Canadian sailors, share these views.
The two unions fear that the Canadian coasting trade will be taken by storm by ships bearing new names, and operated by American equipment and crews.
While the American marine industry was exerting considerable pressure to prevent our merchant marine from gaining access to the domestic market of the United States, the Government of Canada introduced Bill C-52 providing that the coasting trade in Canadian waters would be reserved to Canadian ships.
On the one hand, when the Bill was before the House, we underlined the fact that allowing ships under foreign flags to take part in shipping activities in Canadian costal waters because of a lack of Canadian ships constituted a dangerous concession to foreign, and especially to American shippers.
On the other hand, it was perhaps even more appropriate to state as we did that the Conservative Government had picked a very bad time to propose amendments to the Canada Shipping Act and that it should have dealt with this issue much earlier during its mandate, in 1985 or 1986. A few weeks later, the Minister of Transport confirmed our views when he ordered that the hearings of the Legislative Committee on Bill C-52 be suspended until completion of the Free Trade Agreement.
The problem is now very serious. According to the allegations of the American shippers to the effect that any new legislation or amendment to existing statutes should provide national treatment for the other country, if Bill C-52 receives passage after ratification of the Free Trade Agreement,
Canada would have to grant national treatment to American shipping companies.
That is the problem. Thus, through its neglect, the Conservative Government has treatened the plausibility of a reform of Canadian shipping legislation based on national prerogatives and is now running the risk of letting the American companies take over our shipping industry because of its delay in providing adequate legislation for our own industry.
Last Friday, when replying to my questions, the Minister said that the United States had refused to budge on certain points. One of these points was the shipping industry. At the very worst, the status quo would be maintained. I say that the status quo is unacceptable. It represents a total failure on the part of the Minister of Transport, who is well known for his jokes, but it is clear today that the Canadian shipping industry is not laughing. It is horrified by the incompetence of this Minister.
The crux of the problem resides in the fact that the text of the first schedule and of the later version could provide easier access to Canada in the future for American coasting vessels while the Canadian shipping industry could not have access to the American market.
There is no need to remind the House that the Canadian shipping industry is entirely owned by Canadians, and it has been stupidly sacrificed to get a Free Trade Agreement with the United States. This is most unfortunate since, of all Canadian industries, it is the best suited to compete with the Americans. While our shipping industry costs absolutely nothing to Canadian taxpayers, the American industry is strongly subsidized, receiving some $270 million a year.
Following a Free Trade Agreement with the United States, there would be a serious imbalance: First, the Americans will be able to own Canadian companies while the reverse will be impossible. Second, the Americans will be able to sell duty free in Canada ships built for them, while it will be impossible under any conditions to sell Canadian built ships in the United States. Third, ships sailing under the Stars and Stripes will be able to request, and in some cases obtain, exemptions from the Canadian legislation to carry out their operations in Canada, and once more, the reverse will be impossible.
No wonder Mr. Norman Hall, President of the Dominion Marine Association, asked that negotiations on transportation issues in the Canada-U.S. free trade talks be suspended for 90 days because the current wording is too lopsided in favour of the Americans. Mr. Hall warned that elimination of the duty over a 10-year period as proposed in the free trade agreement would end up wiping out Canadian companies. It would mean Americans will set up shipping companies in Canada with duty free U.S. built 1,000 foot ships offering cheaper rates because of their size compared to the smaller 750-foot Canadian built vessels. Trade on the Great Lakes between Canada and the
November 27, 1987

U.S. is now 90 per cent controlled by Canadian shipping companies, but that will change rapidly in the future in favour of the Americans.
Mr. Hall also fears the free trade deal will negate the effects of the coastal trade Bill, an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act, which would extend the exclusive right of Canadian vessels' access to work offshore up to 200 miles from the current 12 miles. The free trade deal will ultimately give American supply vessels to the oil rigs in those waters too. It is now clear to me that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), our captain, has abandoned the ship.

Now I should like to comment briefly on rail transport. During the hearings on Bill C-18, both CN and CP expressed deep concern over the consequences which the implementation of competitive rail line rates might have on their financial viability in the coming years. Pursuant to Bill C-18, a captive shipper might ask a carrier to take goods to a junction point where he might benefit from a cheaper rate offered by another carrier who would transport such goods to their final delivery point.
The rail companies consider that competitive rail line rates are the most serious threat to their own financial viability. In their testimony before the Standing Committee on Transport the management of both companies raised objections to this open-door competitiveness and to the option Canadian shippers would thus have to deal directly with American rail companies. The way they saw it, such conditions would entail a sharp decline in revenue, and that in turn would make railroads increasingly dependent on the Americans and, more particularly, force them to slash capital expenditures just to stay in business.
Responding to such concerns, the Government went along with a suggestion made by the Hon. Member for Lachine-an amendment which, after review, would allow for partly or totally suspending competitive rail line rates. The amendment, a new clause, reads as follows in Bill C-18:
Where, as a result of a review conducted pursuant to section 266 or 267, it is found in a report submitted under either of those sections that the financial viability of Canadian railway companies has been seriously affected by the operation of sections 134 to 142, the Governor in Council may, by order, suspend the operation of those sections, either entirely or with respect to such kinds of traffic as are specified in the order, whereupon those sections cease to be in force, entirely or with respect to the specified kinds of traffic, during such period as is specified in the order or until the order is revoked.
At the time we commended the Government for its decision even though we did not feel it went far enough, for we looked at it as being a constructive measure on the part of a government which, throughout the whole debate on deregulation of transportation in Canada, had seldom abandoned its unflexible and ideological approach. The Reagan-Mulroney Agreement would seem to jeopardize the continued existence of this modest guarantee. Should a transportation annex along the
Supply
lines of the two other texts we have examined so far be implemented, it seems U.S. railway companies would be exempted from the provision on competitive line rates according to Section B of Article 11(2), which reads as follows:
In case of amendments to, or subsequent adoption of measures pursuant to existing measures, which would increase differences or discrimination against national enterprises of the parties, persons and companies of the other party must be given national treatment in the activity sectors suffering additional discrimination or different treatment.
If the final text contained such provisions, any study concluding that the viability of Canadian railway companies is in serious jeopardy because of competition from American railways as a result of competitive line rates, would in itself be an exercise in futility. In this kind of situation, suspending competitive line rates would actually mean applying a new measure in line with existing measures, which might increase differences or discrimination against the parties' nationals and require the application of national treatment to individuals and companies of the other party.
This is at complete variance with the official position taken in Ottawa, according to which all measures contained in Canadian statutes will remain unchanged. Once again, the Canadian Government has caved in to the Americans, and our conclusion must be that the Canadian railways will lose out under the Reagan-Mulroney Agreement.
In concluding, I would like to comment briefly on the trucking question, where again it is quite clear the Government has abdicated its responsibility, under pressure from the powerful American lobby. We know, since we asked the Minister of State (Transport) (Mrs. Vezina) whether Canadian truckers would be protected under the Free Trade Agreement. This week the Minister of State (Transport) was unable to give us a straight answer: "Yes, the truckers will be protected". She beat endlessly around the bush, without giving us any formal assurances in this respect.
I must say we are convinced, considering the eagerness of the American Trucking Association to see this Free Trade Agreement finalized, that the winners are going to be the U.S. trucking companies.
Interestingly, U.S. public opinion originally thought that the Agreement would give U.S. air carriers and truckers access to the Canadian market, and that in exchange, Canadian merchant shipping would have access to trade in U.S. coastal and inland waters. Now it seems the American shipping industry has thrown a wrench in the works, and that Canada is losing across the board as far as transportation is concerned. It loses in the trucking industry, it loses in the shipping industry, and it is losing in the railway sector. The only sector where it has not lost out, and only because that particular sector was completely excluded from the free trade talks, is in the air transportation industry. However, it can hardly be said to be making progress either. As we know, the present situation in the air transportation sector clearly favours the U.S. companies, at the expense of our Canadian companies.

November 27, 1987

I may say, in concluding, that the Conservative Government has failed to do its duty in the transportation industry. It is too bad that a Government that has two Ministers-one Minister of Transport and one Minister of State-to defend the interests of the transportation industry in Canada, has been unable to achieve better results. Here we have two Ministers I judge to be totally incompetent, and who should hand in their resignations as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
As usual, I enjoyed listening to the Hon. Member speaking through his hat. He always gets his material and authoritative sources from the Americans. He spoke today of the latest version of the transport annex although it was an agreed upon annex. He knows full well that the annex from which he was quoting and which he is trying to convince the Canadian people is the final version was released by the Americans. It is their version of the annex but has not been agreed to yet. It is totally false to say that that is a factual document which indicates what will happen in the transportation annex.
We all know that the United States uses the tactic of releasing things to the public early. They enjoy watching the Liberal and New Democratic Parties grab on to these things. We saw it with some so-called secret briefing notes that were prepared two weeks before the agreement was signed. Of course, the Opposition read them with great fanfare in the House, but they did not bear any resemblance to the agreement that was signed.
The same is true in this case, with negotiations in public and using tactics like releasing the text of the annex. Our approach to negotiation is not to lay out our cards to the public, because it simply does not work. The Hon. Member knows that because he has been involved in negotiations. He did not negotiate in public when he had that responsibility.
He also knows that we have a sectoral advisory committee on transportation which is kept up to date and very much involved in what is happening with these negotiations.
The point I want to make is that the Liberals and New Democrats always take information from the United States as their authoritative source.
Who is kowtowing to them?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
No one is kowtowing to anyone at all. As Canadians come to understand the agreement, it is obvious that support is increasing.
We have not kowtowed to anyone. As a matter of fact, I believe that we had in Simon Reisman the top negotiator anywhere in negotiating this agreement with the United States. The Liberals and the NDP attack the man all the time, but he negotiated a pretty good agreement 22 years ago, which the Liberals will admit, and he will not see that agreement
jeopardized. The fact is that he has negotiated a very good agreement for Canada.
The opposition Parties continually quote the Americans and talk about the annex as if it had been approved and was in place. Why do they keep doing this? Why do they not listen to Canadians? Why do they not wait until they see the annex before they make these unfounded criticisms?

Mr. Speaker, I will tell the Parliamentary Secretary that the only information we are able to obtain is the information that is made public by the American authorities. The Government has been secretive about this deal. It is absolutely unbelievable. What does the Conservative Government have to hide?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Nothing.
Why do you not release your documents like the Americans are doing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Because it has not been decided on.
The Conservatives have made a bad deal and they are trying to keep it secret because they know the public will realize how bad it is if it comes out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Not true.

The Government is the lowest in the polls. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) needed something because it was a question of life or death for him. He absolutely needs this deal. It was the only thing that could possibly salvage his political future, so he made the deal with the Americans.
It is a terrible deal. During the last 20 minutes I dealt specifically with the transportation field and how it is clearly a bad deal for that sector.
The Parliamentary Secretary totally avoided the discussion on transportation. He said it is a good deal and we should not rely on the American documentation because it is not yet finalized.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Exactly.
Are the negotiations continuing or not? We were told that the negotiations had been terminated.
That is not true.

It is not true? So we do not have a deal, then. What are you bragging about? Do we or do we not have a deal?
On the one hand we have a deal, but the negotiations are not finished. What are the Conservatives talking about? They are trying to mislead the population. Either you have a deal or not. If you do not have a deal, you are misleading the Premiers by trying to make them believe that the deal has been concluded.
November 27, 1987

There is no doubt that this is a terrible deal in the field of transportation. Neither the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) nor the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Vezina) have been able to articulate what is good for the Canadian transportation domain. On the contrary, the Minister of Transport said that he is disappointed because he has not been able to obtain what he has been trying to achieve.
We know that he already gave up a lot in the railway sector and trucking areas in order to obtain a breakthrough with the abolition of the Jones Act.
There is no doubt that the Parliamentary Secretary does not know what he is talking about when he suggests that people support the deal. The Dominion Marine Association, the Canadian Trucking Association, and the Canadian Bus Association have all come out strongly against the free trade agreement as it has been presented to them so far, and they are asking the Government to suspend the drafting of the annex for 90 days in order for them to have an input in trying to change it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: They have an input.

If they want to change it, it is certainly because it is no good.
I want the Minister of State for Transport to try to answer the very specific questions I asked earlier and to show us if she knows something about transport.

Mr. Speaker, as we have just witnessed from this exchange, when it comes to talking through one's hat, the Parliamentary Secretary is a master and champion.
My question to the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) relates to statements made by R.J. Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear that half a million Canadian workers are in danger-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: He has no faith in Canadians. Typical Liberals.

Mr. Speaker, I want you to realize that despite the noise and reaction of Conservative Members, it is not me who is saying this. It is Canadian businessmen and the transport industry who are saying clearly that the action of the Conservative Government jeopardizes their industry. Clearly that is what it is. Therefore, I want to confirm what the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) said, that, indeed, through the competitive line rates, the American railways are going to get an unjust advantage over the Canadian railways.
I see it is very painful for the Conservatives when we get to specific points. It is painful for them to have to talk specifically about the free trade deal. They would rather make those nice long speeches on the future of the country. But the future of the country is in relation to jobs and security of employment in some sectors. The responsible people in the transport industry are saying that because of this Government thousands of jobs will be lost to the Americans.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Minister of State (Transport) (Mrs. Vezina).

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted with the opportunity the Opposition is giving the House today to consider the question of free trade and the transportation industry. At last the Opposition has decided to drop all pretences. In fact, I think genuine congratulations are in order here.
In the motion before the House today, the Opposition has decided to come clean.
During the past week, they have been trying to scare our partners in the transportation industry and the general public. However, the wording of today's motion is a clear indication they do not really want to talk about free trade. They want to challenge the whole deregulation process started by this Government. I would like to get back to that in a few moments. First of all, I would like to reiterate my congratulations, and I do so as I would to any other person taking part in a discussion on a committee, with a minimum of intellectual honesty.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress the very ironic dimensions of what we have seen in this House during the past week. I must admit it is not very easy to understand the position the Liberal Party has taken on free trade. Its ideology on this very important issue is certainly not crystal clear. Once I finally managed to make some sense of their abstruse statements, I reached the conclusion that they were against the Agreement.

November 27, 1987
Supply
However, during the past week, the Opposition has been indignant about the fact that no substantial progress had been made in our free trade talks with United States with respect to the transportation sector. Mr. Speaker, I am looking for a modicum of logic in their position and I cannot find it. 1 keep telling myself there must be some consistency in their political thinking. But although I keep trying, I have not been able to find any. Unless, Mr. Speaker, this whole uproar is nothing but a lot of crocodile tears. In either case, Mr. Speaker, I find the situation opposite sad and depressing.
Mr. Speaker, in the past few days the Minister of Transport has said repeatedly in the House that we had not yet signed the agreement on transportation, that our negotiators were still working on it and that the transportation industry did not have to worry about its interests being sacrificed. It seems to me that is a as clear a statement as you can get from the Minister of Transport. There is certainly no room for ambiguity here.
However, Hon. Members opposite will not hear of it. They put their fingers in their ears and keep repeating all kinds of nonsense.
As I said earlier, today the Opposition has come clean. It is not challenging free trade but the whole deregulation of the transportation industry we started and which was put into effect by the National Transportation Act, 1986, and the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1987, Bill C-18 and Bill C-19.
With his usual sense of style and proverbial courtesy, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) was suggesting last Tuesday that since I was so new to Transport, they should cut my pay.
Mr. Speaker, the most accurate statement made in the House during the past week was that I was indeed new to the Department of Transport and that I had brought with me some fresh ideas.
Fully absorbed in the activities of my other departments, I had not had much time to immerse myself in these issues. I should like to remind him, however, that as a representative of a distant riding, I have a gut knowledge of their importance. In my remarks, therefore, I want to bear witness to a situation.
I am amazed at the quality of the legislation which my Government has introduced in this most vital area of our economy.
Regulations were about to choke our transport industry under the previous Government,-the only one in the history of mankind which had managed to lose money with a lottery,-and we were about to sink. When we came into office 1984, we changed all that.
I refer Members opposite to our basic documents, including Freedom to Move, where we clearly defined the principles behind our action: First, less Government interference. This is a concept which the Liberals and to an ever greater degree the NDPs will never be able to understand. The type of Canada they foresee would be an enormous bureaucratic structure
where the Government would control everything in all areas of activities and where, year after year, it would do its utmost to increase the deficit.
The second principle involved in Freedom to Move: Greater reliance on competition and wider range of services to the public.
Again, two notions to which the Opposition is simply impervious. Why on earth should we be concerned about Canadian consumers? Why should we care about Canadian corporations which need efficient transportation services to remain competitive, to preserve existing jobs and create new ones?
Mr. Speaker, the callousness of our colleagues opposite to the needs of consumers is nothing new. I refer for instance to the urea-formaldehyde foam insulation problem. The previous Government spent over six years to try and solve the UFFI problem Canadian consumers were confronted with. At the time, the Liberal Government had done everything in its power to deny is responsibility in this regard. I am told that the UFFI case should be listed in the Guinness Book of Records because it is the one which required the most time to be settled and remained for the longest period before the courts. We, on the contrary, intend to pay very much attention to consumers. We take care of consumers and listen to their needs.
The third principle behind our action is our will to limit restrictive regulation and red tape. Again, this is a principle which is entirely foreign to the daily concerns of people opposite. But we are concerned, because the public expects this type of action.
The Government has incorporated these principles in Bills C-18 and C-19, and I am proud to be part of such a Government. The Opposition is going nowhere with its rearguard fights on legislation already adopted.
I should like now to deal with the various questions raised this week by the Opposition in the area of transport and free trade. Indeed, they are summarized quite well in this motion.
First, Mr. Speaker, you do not have to be Einstein to realize that more trade between Canada and the United States will mean an increased movement of goods, and by extension, more transport. It is therefore obvious that one of the indirect effects of the Free Trade Agreement can only be very beneficial for the transport industry, as well as for all Canadians and all our industries.
Let us now look at each mode of transport seperately, starting with trucking. The Hon. Member for Papineau stated this week that the American transport companies would have unlimited access to the Canadian market while the boundaries of 43 American states would remain closed to our trucking companies. This is unaccurate, Mr. Speaker. Even after looking carefully through all the files of Transport Canada, we were unable to find a single case of a Canadian company which would have been denied the priviledge of operating a branch in one of those states.
November 27, 1987

Mr. Speaker, the Opposition conjures up ghosts and becomes convinced that they are real, then it begins to get scared and to scare the Canadian public. Mr. Speaker, this is ridiculous, intolerable and unacceptable.
The truth is that all Canadian transport companies have benefitted enormously from the deregulation of trucking in the United States. Over 1,000 Canadian companies now operate with enormous success in the United States. Coming back from Quebec City yesterday, I travelled with an owner who told me how effective our policy is and how he had enjoyed unrestricted access to the United States for several years.
Let us now look at railway transport. The Opposition makes a lot out of a statement by Mr. Ritchie, Vice President of the Canadian Pacific, to the effect that we have implemented a one way free trade system with the United States which benefits only the Americans. Of course, the comment of Mr. Ritchie has nothing to do with the Free Trade Agreement, and everything to do with Section 134 of Bill C-18 on competitive line rates. Mr. Ritchie prefered the lack of competition and captive markets, which is easy to explain. The only problem is that the ones to suffer would be the Canadian workers. We have opened up this sector to the Canadian companies because it was in our best interests to do so. I am very sorry if that does not please everyone. As a Government, we were simply unwilling to sacrifice the interests of the many to please Mr. Ritchie.
Let us now talk about maritime transport. I have a double interest in that sector. First, my region, the lower Saint-Lawrence and the Gaspe peninsula, has always been associated with the sea. Second, when I was with the Department of Supply and Services, I became quite familiar with the difficulties of the Canadian shipbuilding industry.
The maritime situation of our country raises many challenges, including the provision of efficient and economical shipping services to support Canadian trading activities. In 1985, over 325 million tons of goods were moved by ship in Canada, and this volume increased to just under 335 million tons in 1986. Of the $115 billion of goods exported last year, over 20 per cent were shipped by sea.
Protectionism is a threat to international maritime trade and to the position of Canada on world markets. Mr. Speaker, our Government is committed to promote free competition in international maritime transport, in spite of the problems caused by protectionism.
This is why, in the Free Trade Agreement negociations, we have tried to convince the Americans to amend their coasting trade regulations under the famous Jones Act. Under this Americam law any vessel plying American coastal waters must have been built in the U.S., be over 75 per cent owned by American interests, and bear the American flag.
As protectionist measures go, these are hard to beat, and I am sure all Ffon. Members would agree. As it stands now the American maritime sector is fully protected. Our situation in
Supply
Canada is different. Among other things, we do not force Canadian shippers to buy vessels built in Canadian shipyards. They are free to buy abroad, but then there is a 25 per cent levy.
Sad though it may be, the Americans were adamant and would not make any concession. I deplore this fact, but that is the way it is. They are sticking with the Jones Act, and that is their right. We too Canadians had non-negotiable sectors, and Members opposite are fully aware of them. One of the very legitimate concerns of the Canadian shipbuilding industry is of course the fact that under the free trade agreement all tariffs between Canada and the United States will disappear over the next ten years, and that includes the 25 per cent rate applicable to foreign-built vessels.
Because we share the industry's concern, we have announced that the Government will not sign an agreement which might prove to be unfavourable to the national interest. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and other Ministers have so assured the House on a number of occasions.
In addition, as the Minister of Transport explained last Tuesday, Bill C-52 on coasting trade and commercial marine activities makes it possible for us to offer even more protection to Canadian maritime interests and our own shipbuilding industry. We will not hesitate to use that mechanism should it ever become necessary to do so. Mr. Speaker, I would remind you that the Bill was adopted last May 1, and it is aimed at rationalizing and updating the process of eligibility for coastal trade. Regulatory procedures will be streamlined so that owners of Canadian vessels will no longer have to secure a coastal trade permit.
The Bill also restricts coastal trade activities to vessels flying the Canadian flag and goes on to define the activities covered by these provisions as well as the extent of it application. More specifically, henceforth Canada's coastal trade regulations will apply 200 instead of 12 miles offshore as a result of Bill C-52. A system of exemptions is in place to ensure that adequate maritime services respond to the needs of Canadians.
The Bill has gone through second reading and been referred to committee, and we intend to complete its study and, indeed, have it adopted.
Mr. Speaker, to sum up the situation concerning the liberalization of trade with respect to maritime transport services, I would say there has been no progress. speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

subtopic: LANGUAGE TRAINING POLICY-SITUATION OF IMMIGRANT WOMEN
LANGUAGE TRAINING POLICY-SITUATION OF IMMIGRANT WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 1981 Census statistics showed that almost 50 per cent more immigrant women than men had no knowledge of either official language. The main reason for this deplorable statistic is the federal Government's policy on subsidized language training for immigrants. This policy clearly disadvantages women. Immigrant women, who may not be working in the labour force, are certainly working in the home and they need to communicate in one of the official languages to function efficiently in their daily lives.
Immigrant women who are seeking to enter the workforce are also often denied access to language training, as it is judged that the few marketable job skills they possess will make them ineligible for employment that requires communication abilities.
The result is that immigrant women, especially those from developing countries, are ghettoized in low-paying menial jobs. We know that this only reinforces the sexist and the racist stratification of our society that keeps women of visible minority groups in poverty, and powerless in our society.

ESTABLISHMENT OF PRINCE EDWARD COUNTY MARINE PARK ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, off the shores of Prince Edward County in the deep, dark, cold waters of Lake Ontario lies a treasure of untold value. Over 200 ships of every shape and type known in the late 1800s sank in these waters at a time when the lakes, bays and rivers were the main routes of commerce in Upper Canada.
Many ships went down during the barley days, that time in the history of Prince Edward County when every possible acre of land was covered with the golden crop, usually shipped out to make beer and ale.
Deep Quest II, a highly respected voluntary organization, has researched and photographed many of these ships. It now hopes to set up an underwater habitat in the area to further its scientific exploration.
Canada has already recognized the value of underwater marine parks and I have initiated talks along these lines with the Minister responsible for Parks Canada. Unless they are properly protected, these vignettes of Canadian history could be vandalized for souvenirs as happened to the Titanic this summer.
I ask for and indeed look forward to the co-operation of all my colleagues in establishing the necessary facilities to protect these old ships while at the same time making an exciting part of Canada's history available to all Canadians.

My constituents state that whereas since September, 1984 the federal Government has imposed on Canadian taxpayers 25 new taxes or tax increases, in particular on medical and dental supplies, snack foods, candies, and soft drinks; and whereas the federal Government in its tax reform proposals is studying the possibility of imposing on Canadians a general tax on goods and services including foods; and whereas food constitutes a vital element in the day-to-day life and the

November 27, 1987

imposition of this tax would have the effect of seriously penalizing certain categories of taxpayers such as the aged, families, the unemployed, youth, and low income taxpayers; wherefore, the undersigned petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject all measures that would have the effect of imposing a sales tax on food products, and as duty bound your petitioners ever pray.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I have 10 petitions in all from across my riding, and indeed some visitors from Montreal and Quebec have signed these petitions, and 1 ask leave to present the same in their names.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have petitions signed by residents of my constituency of Thunder Bay-Nipigon, by residents of other communities in northwestern Ontario, and indeed by a few visitors to the region from other parts of Canada.
The petitioners note that the federal Government's White Paper calls for changes to the taxation structure of Canada, but those proposals do not change an already unfair tax structure for average Canadian families. They allow wealthy Canadians earning more than $100,000 a year to continue not paying their fair share and to actually receive a tax cut under the proposals. These proposals will also allow 60,000 profitable corporations to continue paying no income tax.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to reject these tax changes, and particularly to reject the proposed tax on food. They call on Parliament to restore full indexation to the personal tax system.

speechtext: For questions and comments on the speech by the Minister of State (Transport) (Mrs. Vezina). The Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet).

Mr. Speaker, I may remind the Minister of State (Transport) (Mrs. Vezina) of the remarks I directed to her earlier this week, on November 23, when 1 said, as reported at page 11067 of Hansard:
... I would like to put a question to the Minister of State (Transport) as she did not reply to the very simple questions asked earlier by my colleague for Westmorland-Kent.
I would like to give her an opportunity to prove that she is worthy of her pay and that she knows something about her new Department.
That is what I said, and when I listened to her earlier, she mentioned certain reproaches which I never made. If she would care to stick to the facts as printed in Hansard, the only reproach I made was that she did not reply to the questions put to her in the House. The Hon. Member for Westmorland- Kent (Mr. Robichaud) asked two questions last week which she failed to answer. I put two questions to the Minister myself, and she did not answer them. Today, we have had another example. The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) asked her a very simple question. Again, she failed to answer the question. She took the question as notice.
I maintain that in the circumstances, it would be normal for the Hon. Member, who has ministerial responsibilities, who has a duty to take part in Question Period and defend the
November 27, 1987

Government's point of view and answer the questions put to her by the Opposition, to do her job.
That was my reproach. I never commented on her age, courtesy or style, and I wish she would stick to what I said in the Elouse.
Furthermore, I would like to ask the Minister whether she had time to consult with her departmental officials, and if so, whether she could give me a straight answer to the question 1 asked. The question was simple. I told her: All you have to say is yes or no. She has yet to do so. I want to know whether or not, after this free trade agreement is signed with the United States, whether or not the Canadian provinces will have the right to deny a licence to American truckers headquartered in a State which does not give fair treatment to our truckers. That is the question that I put to her. She has not answered it yet. For the third time, I ask whether the Canadian provinces will have the right to deny a licence to American truckers from States which do not grant the same access to Canadian truckers, yes or no? That is my question.
I will conclude by saying that in that part of the text prepared by officials from the Department of Transport that was read by the Minister of State (Transport), I recognize exactly the same criticism that we have been expressing, namely that the Government must admit that American railways have been granted advantages that are denied to Canadian railways. The Minister had to admit that fact earlier this morning.
Secondly, the Minister had to admit that Americans have resisted all attempts to ease the restrictions in the area of shipping and that the status quo will prevail. However, that status quo is not encouraging for the Canadian shipping industry. On the contrary, the status quo-together with the free trade agreement which will grant national treatment to American shipping companies- will favour American shippers companies to the detriment of Canadian shippers.
Finally, spokesmen for various trucking associations in Canada, including Mr. Raymond Cope, president of the Ontario Trucking Association, Mr. Ron Downey, president of the Manitoba Trucking Association, and Mr. Don Norquay, president of Manitoba's Motor Transport Board, have all said that changes should have been made to fiscal laws and immigration laws before we sign a trade agreement with the Americans, and that this proposed agreement will not allow Canada to take effective measures in order to prevent Americans from having total control of the trucking industry. These people are directly involved in the area of trucking and they ought to know what they are talking about.
For these reasons, 1 cannot understand how the Minister can rise in this House and say that in the area of transportation this Mulroney-Reagan agreement could be good for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I concluded my speech earlier by wishing that, during

the many years I intend spending in this House, I will no longer see as much ambiguity, complexity and confusion as in the comments we have bean hearing, especially this week, about the transport industry.
While the truckers know what they are talking about, I must unfortunately say that the Members opposite do not quite know what they are talking about when they ask questions such as those we heard this week in this House.
When I was reviewing this week's activities, I saw quite clearly that the Opposition wanted mostly to speak about deregulation, which they refuse to accept. They ask questions under the pretext of speaking about free trade.
As for me, the question I would like to ask the Hon. Member opposite is this: When will he stop scaring people with his unfounded and unrealistic fears?
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) clearly told us this week that the part of the Agreement which relates to transport has not yet been signed. Our negotiators are working on it. Our transport industry should not be afraid that we might sacrifice its interests. As a responsible Government, we shall evaluate everything and refuse to sign any agreement which could sacrifice national interests.
Let Members opposite really speak about free trade and the transport industry in this House, and we shall reply to their questions. Moreover, when the time comes to speak about deregulation, we shall reply to their questions about that issue as well.
However, we fully realize that all the questions asked this week were aimed at provoking confusion in Canada.
We are clearly preserving the existing situation and unfortunately maintaining the status quo as far as the transport industry is concerned. Our Government had decided on behalf of Canadians that certain sectors were non-negotiable. The Americans had decided not to negotiate and not to accept our offers. They were fully entitled to act as they did. As I have said, we shall always try to protect the interests of Canadians.
I find it very hard to understand that the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) cannot accept a very simple and clear principle: The more trade there is between Canada and the United States, the greater the movement of goods will be, which means more transport.
I have already pointed out that 1 made some research this week and found that, among the 1,000 companies which already operate in the United States, not a single one had been penalized by the existing mechanisms.
Let the Opposition deal with the free trade issue and we shall reply to their questions!

Mr. Speaker. 1 am delighted that the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) has moved this motion. However, I find it somewhat amusing and ironic that he has done so since his Party is the one that started all this-Mr. Speaker, I wonder if my colleague would be good enough to go over there, sit down and talk with the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Vezina) there rather than-well, I will just sit down and wait until they are finished.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) has the floor.
I can talk to my colleague.

Go over there and do it. Quit yacking away while I am trying to make my speech. I did not interrupt yours.
Now you can begin counting my time, Mr. Speaker.
I started to say that I am happy that the hon. gentleman from Papineau has moved this motion, although I find it somewhat ironic and amusing that he has done so since the Party he represents is the one that started all this. It is the one that came out with deregulation. When he was Minister of Transport, the late unlamented Otto Lang started all this in 1975. Of course, there is a perfectly logical reason for the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) not being the transport critic for the Liberal Party. He is the one who started deregulation by drafting such legislation for the House of Commons.
I am assuming that the Liberal Party has had a change of heart about deregulation, particularly as it pertains to the free trade agreement. I find that this motion is accurate and correct and I would like to deal with each part of the motion that has been put by the Hon. Member for Papineau.
The Government refused to listen to representatives of the trucking industry. The Canadian Trucking Association and all its provincial affiliates are not only angry about Bill C-18, the new National Transportation Act, but they are also outraged by the results of the melding of deregulation and the free trade deal.
I respect the Minister of State for Transport and think she is competent. I listened very carefully to her speech. I expected her to reply in detail to each of the points made in the motion, but she did not.
It is true, as indicated in paragraph 1 of the motion, that the Canadian trucking industry is faced, not only with the laws of the U.S. Government and the constitutional authority of the U.S. Congress, Senate and House of Representatives, but it is faced with the regulations of 43 individual states of the United States. I know that the Minister of State for Transport is competent, but I wish she would inform herself on these
particular items and respond to them. If we are wrong, she should point out exactly where we are wrong.
I was amused today during Question Period when government Members asked why we had not read the information they had provided. I have yet to receive the transportation annex to the free trade deal from a government Member or from anyone eise in Canada. We did get it from the publication entitled Inside U.S. Trade, not an American government publication but a private publication that we were able to obtain in order to read the transportation annex to the free trade deal.
The Canadian trucking industry, railways, airlines and marine industry is faced with exactly what they have been faced with before, only the situation is worse now. They are faced with more than what they were faced with before. Here is a paragraph out of the transportation annex:
Neither party shall be under any obligation to change existing measures relating to the provision of transportation services that accord persons of the other party treatment that is less favourable than that accorded to its own persons.
I believe you, Sir, were at the committee hearings on a number of occasions when we were dealing with Freedom to Move and Bill C-18 and Bill C-19. That is exactly what we said in the committee then. It is exactly what the Canadian Truckers Association and the railroads said then and are saying now. I tried my best to persuade the Government to accept amendments to those two Bills which would allow Canada to take reciprocal measures or, as I put it in committee: We will do unto you what you do unto us. The Government refused to accept those amendments.
We are now faced with a situation where U.S. truckers can do things in Canada that Canadian truckers cannot do in the U.S. The U.S. truckers have advantages under tax laws, mean labour laws, and individual state regulations, that Canadian truckers have to compete with. When they talk about a level playing field, even if it is level, the problem is that the U.S. has the ball on the 10-yard line with three downs to go. However, it is our 10-yard line!
Dealing with the railroads' competitive line rates and Bill C-18, Canadian Pacific and Canadian National told the committee and the Government publicly that they supported deregulation. However, once they got the fine print and once they got the Bill, they changed their minds, for perfectly good reasons.
Paragraph two of this motion refers to Canadian law providing for competitive line rates. That is not only not provided for in the U.S. on their railroads, it is prohibited. When Canadian railroads say that billions of dollars in revenue are subject to what they call a licence to raid by American railroads and American trucking companies, they are perfectly right. They have good reason to be angry and fearful. We gave away the store in Bill C-18 and compounded
November 27, 1987

it by confirming it in the transportation annex of the free trade deal.
The issue of Canadian airlines failing to receive equitable treatment in the U.S. is long-standing. The free trade deal and the new transportation laws under so-called deregulation in Canada make no move whatsoever to correct that unfair treatment. It is perfectly logical that the U.S. is interested only in flying to five or six places in Canada. Since they have more than 10 times our population, obviously Canadian airlines would like to go to 20 or 30 places in the U.S. However, you can bet your bottom dollar, free trade deal or not, there is no way the U.S. is going to allow it. Anyone who thinks otherwise is suffering from sheer delusion.
The Marine Industry Association and all those connected with marine shipping and manufacturing in Canada initially supported free trade. They bought a pig in a poke just like so many others. They believed the U.S. would agree to apply the Jones Act and all its amendments to Canadian shipping. It has not. Canada is still excluded from fair treatment in the U.S., but the U.S. industry can do things in Canada that ours cannot do there. That is not a level playing field, never was and never will be, under this deal and the laws of Canada or the United States.
Regardless of what the free trade deal says, we need a clause in our legislation which permits the Government of Canada to take reciprocal action, whether it be in the trucking industry, marine industry, airline industry or railway industry. Anything the Americans do to us, we do exactly the same to them. To lay back and enjoy it while leaving ourselves wide open to the siphoning off of transportation revenues to American companies is surely a sell-out of some kind.
At one point the Minister of State for Transport said in her speech that over 1,000 trucking companies from Canada operate in the U.S. She is right. They have anywhere from one truck to a couple of hundred. Yet if it is working, why try to fix it? Since nothing has been achieved in the free trade deal to get rid of the unfair advantages that American truckers have over Canadian truckers, whether it is here or in the U.S., then it is not a fair deal. Why did the Minister not address that?
In response to the Hon. Member for Papineau, she said her Government will not sacrifice transport interests. I suggest to you that the Government has already done that in Bill C-18 and Bill C-19. It has done nothing in the free trade deal to correct the disadvantages that Canadian transporters have in the U.S.
The biggest problem is this outrageous delusion across the country, particularly among the proponents of free trade, but even those worried about it suffer from it as well, that somehow or other the U.S. is going to hold still for Canada, or any other country for that matter, getting a larger share of their market than we already have. We have had countless instances of the U.S. putting in place tariffs, countervailing duties, outright embargoes, or other severe restrictions on our trade and transportation dealings with that country. Now the
Supply
Government claims that if we get a free trade deal we do not have to worry about that any more. The transportation part of the deal throws that in a cocked hat. The annex says, and I will read it again:
Neither party shall be under any obligation to change existing measures
relating to the provision of transportation services that accord persons of the
other party treatment that is less favourable than that accorded to its own
persons.
That means that everything in place now in transportation remains in place under the free trade agreement. I do not want to hear the Minister or anyone else in the Government try to tell us that we are getting a good deal in transportation under the free trade agreement, because we are not. At best, the situation remains the same as it has always been, and it is highly likely to get worse.
People suffer from a delusion about the so-called free trade agreement with the United States. They forget that before the United States agreed to the fast-track it received from the President of the United States a complete and unequivocal assurance that any free trade agreement with Canada would in no way impinge upon the constitutional authority and rights of the United States House of Representatives, the United States Senate, or the rights of the individual states of the United States.
When the transport committee was sitting in Vancouver hearing evidence on the deregulation of transportation I spoke to a trucker who told me that he had a licence to move goods to California, Arizona, Texas, and even Mexico. He said that he had fewer problems with the State of California than with the regulatory regimes and harassment he had to undergo in the states of Oregon and Washington in trying to get to California. That is why I find the first paragraph of this motion perfectly appropriate. There are at least 43 states which have separate regulations.
As officials of the Canadian Trucking Association have said, the implementation of Bill C-19 next January 1 will mean at least a year of chaos. The Government's own uniform national safety code, a uniform code of national regulations, is still not in place. It is still being negotiated with the provinces, and we all know what it is like trying to get the 10 provinces to agree on anything. They cannot even agree on the time of day. Saskatchewan and Newfoundland are examples of that. None of that is in place.
Let us take a look at the situation in western Canada. I heard a government Member talking today about the mining association being all for free trade. Tell that to the potash miners in Saskatchewan. Under the free trade deal the tariff of up to 85 per cent imposed by the United States on Canadian potash remains in place. The Province of Saskatchewan was left no choice other than to impose the tariff itself.
At least we salvaged something under the Western Grain Transportation Act which got rid of the Crow rate. The

November 27, 1987
Supply
national Government still pays a major portion of the cost of moving grain. The grain companies in Saskatchewan and Alberta which have been selling hundreds of thousands of tonnes of screenings, meal, and pellets into the United States will no longer get the benefit of the Western Grain Transportation Act under the free trade agreement.
I can understand that someone from Ontario, including the Parliamentary Secretary, would not know what that is all about. However, our grain producers will lose the benefit of the Western Grain Transportation Act on exports of screenings, meal, and pellets to the United States.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: When?

That takes effect immediately. When we lose the two-price grain system, western grain producers will lose $260 million. I can understand ignorance in people from downtown Toronto or Ottawa who would not know a bushel of wheat if it hit them in the face, but anyone in western Canada who supports a free trade deal which will cost western grain producers $260 million as a result of the loss of the two-price system is guilty of failing to fight for grain producers in western Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: The grain producers love it.

The grain producers do not love it. I wish my hon. friend had been with me at the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool convention last week because he would have got an earful. That organization represents more grain producers than all the other grain organizations in the country put together. The hon. gentleman should go to the next annual meeting of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. He will find himself welcome and he will find out that the western grain producers do not like the free trade deal with regard to the Western Grain Transportation Act and the two-price system.
We gave away the store on potash and grain under the Western Grain Transportation Act and western Canada will lose. The transportation industry in Canada will lose. Our railroads will lose on competitive line rates which American railroads can have in Canada but Canadian railroads cannot have in the United States. The Minister of State for Transport completely failed to respond to that little problem. She never even mentioned it. Our airlines will not get any better treatment from the United States under the free trade deal. The Minister failed to address that at all.
The Minister completely failed to address the clause in this motion about the treatment of the marine industry. We remain in exactly the same disadvantaged position in our marine sector with the United States as we always have. The free trade deal does absolutely nothing to alleviate that. In fact, it entrenches what the Americans have been doing for decades, and there is nothing we can do about it under the free trade deal. The Minister failed to address that specific problem as well.
In conclusion, I know that my hon. friends are just as patriotic as am I and that they love this country as much as anyone else. However, they must not sign this deal until they have taken it to the people of Canada. They must not sign a deal which decreases our sovereignty, independence, and ability to have a level playing field with the United States. I have cited half a dozen instances in which the playing field is not level. Even if it were, the United States has the ball on our 10-yard line with four downs to go. I predict they will continue to do what they have been doing to us repeatedly in so many ways for decades. With regard to transportation, the free trade deal will not only be meaningless to Canada but will be harmful.

Mr. Speaker, first a comment and then a question. I urge the Hon. Member to listen very carefully.
Here is the comment: I realize that today is an opposition day where we are supposed to talk about free trade. The opposition has also chosen to talk about the deregulation started by our Government. This is why this debate is so ambiguous and vague, without real answers. We should be concentrating on the Free Trade Agreement.
I do not know in what language we should say it, whether it is French, English, Spanish, but I will repeat it. We would not sign an Agreement detrimental to the interests of Canadians, I should say Canadian carriers.
My question is this: I would like to know how one can be against free trade? How can one question an agreement which maintains the status quo? That question seems very clear to me. We are keeping the status quo and you are objecting. Should I understand that the New Democratic Party is reassessing its opposition to free trade?

Mr. Speaker, free trade is like motherhood. One opposes it at one's peril. Who would object to a free trade deal that is free and fair?
The Hon. Member failed to answer the specific points raised. The free trade deal as a result of deregulation in Canada does not address the disadvantages to Canadian transportation in the United States and the advantages for U.S. transporters in Canada. I hope that the content of the final text is different from what is in the transportation annex to the free trade agreement. The transportation annex states that articles 84, 85 and 87 of the agreement shall apply to the provision of transportation services and so on. We do not have the final text, so we do not know what is in articles 84, 85 and 87. That is why I did not mention that in my speech.
Subparagraph (1) of the transportation annex, which I read twice in my speech, means that the advantages U.S. truckers have over Canadian truckers remain in place. The Government refused to accept my amendments that would level the playing
November 27, 1987

field under Bill C-18 and Bill C-19. Therefore, we have no way of counteracting actions taken by the U.S. Administration, the Congress or individual states.
I suggest to the Minister that if the Government addresses these problems in transportation, my opposition to this so-called free trade deal may be somewhat lessened. If she can return to the House before December 18 and show how the Government has renegotiated the transportation annex to cover the four areas mentioned in the motion of the Hon. Member for Papineau, to cover the Western Grain Transportation Act and the two-price grain system, then there will be a fair deal. However, it does not exist now. I hope she can do so but I do not think she will.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious as the debate proceeds this afternoon that opposition Members, particularly the Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), have a different vision of what free trade is all about.
We in the Government believe that the free trade agreement will provide advantages to Canadian producers, whether they are farmers, fishermen, tourist operators or truckers.
It is unfortunate, when we have this opportunity to make Canada stronger by virtue of those new markets to which we will have assured access, that the Opposition would suggest the opposite would occur. We want to ensure access to a market just next door which has so many opportunities.
It has been suggested in the debate today that deregulation in the transportation industry will not provide that kind of opportunity. I believe that approach is absolutely wrong. The fear expressed about the Canadian trucking industry simply does not hold water.
There are over 1,000 Canadian trucking firms now operating between Canada and the United States. Many of these have started since deregulation in the United States.
Canadian firms have increased their operations to the United States in recent years, and easier entry into the Canadian market could alter or stabilize the balance of market share. However, if barriers are retained for U.S. truckers in Canada, Canadian truckers then risk losing their access to that lucrative U.S. market.
I suggest that it is not likely that U.S. truckers would dominate the Canadian transporter markets because most of this traffic is short-haul. This is a market where the competitive performance of Canadian firms compares well to that of their American counterparts.
American domiciled employees are presently forbidden by our immigration laws from engaging in domestic trucking in Canada. Regulatory reform will not change this situation. Bill C-18 is designed to enhance the competitiveness of Canadian industry in both domestic and international markets, by controlling transportation costs through market forces. Canadian carriers must share in this endeavour by providing
Supply
efficient, least cost competitive and safe transportation services.
I return to my first comment. If this country is to succeed in the long run it must be competitive. We must have the kind of deregulation that is being proposed in this Bill in order that our industry can compete with any other. We have no fear about our industry being as good as the American industry. This legislation is important to Canada in order to have a bilateral trade deal which will open a market that is 10 times the size of ours.

Mr. Speaker, that is an example of more of the delusion from that side. The market has been open for all these years, in any event. Even the Government says that the United States is our biggest trading partner.
There has been free trade in cattle, hogs, and a host of items. As a result of that, the Americans have imposed countervails and duties.
I am amused by The Cattlemen's Association in Saskatchewan and Alberta, who suffer from what I call the Texas cowboy syndrome. They believe that the United States cattle producers and the packing industry will remain silent while Canada gets a larger share of the market than we already have.
There were some three occasions in the last 15 years when they shut down the border on some other restrictions. The free trade agreement allows them to continue to do the same thing. What kind of deal is that?
I never knew that Canada exported raspberries, but the same thing happened with raspberries twice in the last three years. Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia ship thousands of tonnes of raspberries to the United States. The Americans countervailed our raspberries. Nothing has changed with the free trade deal.
The same provisions will still apply, whether it is with respect to trucking, airlines, rail or marine shipping. I suggest to my hon. friend that he read the transportation annex. Read what it says. It says that neither party shall be under any obligation to change existing measures-existing measures- relating to the provision of transportation services that accord persons of the other party treatment that is less favourable-I repeat, less favourable-than that accorded to its own persons. So nothing has changed. The competitive line rates we have granted to the United States railroads are not available to Canadian railroads in the United States. No one can tell me that Bill C-18 and the free trade deal does anything about that because it does not. It is another instance where we gave away the store.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).

November 27, 1987
