Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate initiated this afternoon by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet). He moved this motion:
That this House condemn the Government for its destructive influence on the Canadian transportation industry by its impractical and slavish adherence to the ideological myth of deregulation and its inept trade negotiations with the United States-
Mr. Speaker, this kind of preamble in the motion by the Hon. Member for Papineau depicts admirably the ineptitude of this Conservative Government. I see the Hon. Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Vezina) sitting across the way. Mr. Speaker, I like the Minister very much. At one time I had the privilege to be her critic in the House. We got along fairly well. I think that she is damaging her own credibility by condoning her government even when it is wrong. She should be more excellent. It would enhance her credibility which is already very high. But she will loose it if she continues to approve the initiatives of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) who lacks a great deal of judgement in transportation issues and nearly all other issues for that matter.
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians worry about the free trade deal concluded by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States. It has already been said today that the shipping industry is deeply worried. The Dominion Marine Association which represents 14 Canadian shipping companies, or 90 per cent of this industry, opposes the deal. The Government told us that this free trade deal was needed in order to find a way to settle trade disputes between our two countries and also to protect and increase our sales and our markets in the United States.
I ask the Minister opposite: what has been done to change the Jones Act, for instance, an American act which for all practical purposes prohibits any foreign investment or profit in the U.S. marine industry? The Minister knows-she said it earlier-that the Jones Act is untouched, that it is a protectionist measure that is almost airtight. It is impossible to amend. The Minister agreed to that. I suppose she will also agree that the Prime Minister's efforts to increase trade, at least in that area, were a complete failure. This is the only possible conclusion, Mr. Speaker. What access do Americans have to Canadian markets? Everyone knows that Canada allows foreign-built ships and up to 100 per cent foreign ownership of a Canadian marine company. Mr. Norman Hall, president of the Dominion Marine Association, said on November 25 that the elimination of the 25 per cent tariff on 1000-foot ships, that is presently in existence and that will stay until the Government eliminates it with its famous free-trade deal, would ruin Canadian companies.
I note that the Minister answered some other questions earlier, but that she ignored this very important issue.
Mr. Speaker, other Canadian industries in the transportation field will be negatively affected.

For instance, we could talk about the railroads. We know, of course, that our rail system was deregulated by Bill C-18, a Bill proposed in this House by the Government of Canada. We also know that it is the same Government which proposed another Bill last year, Bill C-97. Under Bill C-97, a Bill entitled an Act respecting rail passenger transportation, there would be a provision in there to permit the Minister to abandon passenger rail lines without even having a hearing process, under certain circumstances.
I bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, a very important issue for the constituency I represent. As you will know, because you are a very knowledgeable person, the CN train line between Ottawa and Montreal goes through the constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. That rail line is commonly referred to, in railway language, as the Alexandria subdivision. One would think that the rail line linking the Cities of Ottawa and Montreal would be pretty safe from being shut down. That is not so. CN released-not intentionally, of course but made public-a document on September 25, 1986, outlining how it was going to proceed to shut down certain rail lines, one being the Alexandria subdivision between Ottawa and Montreal. That would effectively eliminate all passenger and freight between Ottawa and Montreal. I know you have travelled on that train yourself, Mr. Speaker, and so have many other people, but they will not be able to do that if CN gets its way.
The internal document in question was actually slipped under my door by someone. That is how it was released. That does happen every now and then and, incidentally, I may as well take this occasion now to say to anyone who has any such documents that they would like to slip under my door, I would be always ready to accept them as I have in the past.
This document dated September 25, 1986, signed by Mr. R. P. Langlois, states:
In the context of the rationalization of our rail infrastructure, some lines have been identified as being potential candidates for abandonment in the coming years. A preliminary plan has been prepared and attached you will find the sections affected.
It goes on to say that any effort to attract new traffic on these lines is to be abandoned immediately. In other words, this internal document is telling other functionaries of CN Rail to stop looking for customers, that it wants to shut down.
I have the attached list referred to in the letter which identifies each subdivision and the year CN plans to shut it down. The Alexandria subdivision, a distance of 57.7 miles-pardon me for not using metric-is scheduled to shut down, according to this list, in 1990.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the discovery of this document created quite a debate in the constituency I represent, and I know it did to a certain degree in the riding of Stormont- Dundas as well because that is a neighbouring riding to the one I represent in this House. We had meetings with community groups, all wanting to protest this potential closure. We
November 27, 1987

even had a company in my riding which was prepared to construct a brand new building, a company which has now put all of its plans in abeyance. I am speaking of Alexandria Moulding. The building plan has stopped until the issue of whether or not we keep our rail line is settled since the company is not going to spend money without knowing whether or not it can ship its goods.
Over time we managed to get a commitment from the Government that the rail line would be safe until at least 1992. That is small comfort. The only thing that that has told us is that we are being given an extra two years. It is hardly something that would constitute reassurance for an industry in deciding whether or not to establish in our area.
In any case, on April 10, 1987, Lawrence Hanigan, the defeated Tory candidate in the riding of Laval-des-Rapides, who was subsequently appointed to head VIA Rail, wrote a letter to the Hon. Member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Warner) in which he stated:
As I indicated to you on the telephone, VIA has every intention of maintaining service between Ottawa and Montreal. It is, for that matter, a core service, and would be protected in the service network listed in the schedule attached to the proposed National Rail Passenger Transportation Act.
This National Rail Passenger Transportation Act is Bill C-97. In the annex to the Bill the Alexandria subdivision is listed as a corridor service. Under Clause 14(a) of the Bill a corridor service must recover at least 100 per cent of specific costs. In other words, if it does not break even the Minister has the right to shut it down. That is exactly the problem, it does not break even. So in other words what Mr. Hanigan has told us is, "Don't worry because we will shut it down". That is in fact what Bill C-97 states. Luckily since then the Tories have abandoned Bill C-97 and will apparently bring forward a new Bill in a short period of time. We do not know what it will be like. However, we hope that at least that corridor will be protected, and really protected, not the way it was under the transportation legislation of last year.
I wish to speak briefly about the trucking industry in the riding I represent. The largest single employer in my riding is a company by the name of Glengarry Transport. Glengarry Transport has some 2,000 employees.

That industry owns more than 5000 vehicles and, contrary to what might be thought, it is not a big multinational, nor an American company, nor a company from a big city. In fact, the Glengarry Transport Company, or GTL as it is known in the area, belongs to the Lefebvre family from Alexandria. Thus, it is a family business, a big success which the people of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell are very proud of.
Messrs Poirier and Vaillancourt, the managers of Glengarry Transport, told me in June that, if passed, Bill C-19 would cause their company to cut 20 to 30 per cent of its jobs.
Supply
Imagine, Mr. Speaker, 30 per cent of the 2000 employees would lose their jobs. And why did we pass Bill C-19? Of course, it was to please the Americans, so that they would be willing to sign the Free Trade Agreement. I see a Minister on the other side, and it is interesting to note that that Minister is with us. I hope the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick) is not ill-disposed towards the people in the transport industry. For I know for sure, Mr. Speaker, that the Associate Minister of National Defence is very much ill-disposed towards the workers in the textile industry.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read to you an article by Robert Bousquet, journalist at the daily newspaper Le Droit, which has been published last Monday. Mr. Bousquet interviewed the Associate Minister of National Defence. In particular, he asked the Minister why he favors free trade and so on. He wanted to know whether the Minister was worried about the textile industries. Here is what the Minister replied to those industries: "They had between three and five opportunities of modernizing through governmental programs. Companies that did not seize these opportunities just deserve to close down. It is for democracy: you cannot please everybody. Some will be affected." The article goes on: "Mr. Dick does not see the need for a referendum on free trade. He says: Our mandate was to set the Canadian economy back on foot, and free trade is a means towards that end."
That is the statement made on Monday by the Associate Minister of National Defence. I tell the Minister that his remarks regarding the textile workers, the managers of that industry and the industry as a whole will haunt him from now on because he has no right whatsoever to pretend that his Government has the privilege to decide that some industries are outdated.
This Government, Mr. Speaker, was elected with an overwhelming majority. Yes, we recognize it. It is unfortunate that it was elected with such a majority. Indeed, it is unfortunate that it was elected, period! However, during the election campaign, the gentleman who is now the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) said, and I quote:

"Don't talk to me about free trade. That issue was decided in 1911. Free trade is a danger to Canadian sovereignty. You will hear none of it from me at election time nor at any other time". Those were the words of the man who is now the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) as stated in 1983.
What are we to conclude? That, once again, the Prime Minister gave erroneous information to the Canadian people? And I am trying to be generous here. What are we to think of an Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick) who makes comments about the textile workers such as the ones I have just read from the paper, pretending on the one hand that industries deserve to be shut down while on the other the Government has a mandate to negotiate free trade? One statement is wrong and the other is an outright insult to many constituents, not only those in my riding but in the riding of

November 27, 1987
Supply
Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton as well as in the ridings of Montreal and many other communities around the country. In my riding there are over 3,000 people who work in the textile field. I know that I am digressing slightly from transportation but I am still dealing with free trade. Those people do not appreciate those kinds of remarks that have been made.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude by saying in the few minutes or even seconds I have left that 47 American states still have strong restrictions regarding access of Canadian truckers to their territory. For these Canadian transport firms, increased access to the United States will be difficult if not altogether impossible. Given the appendix introduced earlier by our colleague the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), the transport appendix to the free trade agreement proposed by the Americans, it is evident that if the proposed annex is adopted as it now stands the Canadian transport industry has nothing to gain and everything to lose.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the trucking industry was well advised to ask for this 90 day moratorium and I ask again why the Minister has refused the moratorium.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and his Government owe excuses to the Canadian people for the mess they have just created.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a short comment in view of the fact that the Hon. Member who has just spoken has consistently misrepresented the truth, but there is nothing unusual in the fact that he does not know what he is talking about.
The Hon. Member did not attend the Eastern Ontario Economic Conference at which I spoke on Monday of this week. But as a Member of Parliament from eastern Ontario, perhaps he should have gone there; he may have learned something. There was a lot of representation from people in the municipalities in his constituency, and many other Members of Parliament were there from eastern Ontario. It was a pity that the Hon. Member did not have the interest in his own constituents.
Not once did I make a reference to the workers of the textile industry. 1 made reference once to a textile industry, which was brought up as an example. This textile industry had not modernized over the years, and it was pointed out that it felt that it would not be able to compete. I pointed out that it had been given three five-year programs, the first undertaken by the former Liberal administration in which the textile industry was given special consideration in order that it would be able to put itself into a position to compete. If management had been so poor as not to do that, then I felt sorry for the workers in that industry, but I said that we would have to provide some
transfer of funds in order to ensure that we would be able to get new jobs for them.
It is a pity that the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) always misrepresents the truth in the House. It is a pity for his constituents whom he does not serve well by not even going to the Eastern Ontario Economic Conference. I feel that he should spend more time being a good Member than picking holes and misrepresenting other people's thoughts.

Mr. Speaker, I will gladly respond to that intervention.
First, I do not apologize for having been in the House of Commons on Monday. I was elected to be here. I was doing my job. I was on Parliament Hill at the time that this conference was going on.
The meeting was at lunch time.

Second, the Minister makes this gratuitous comment that that industry in my riding had not modernized. We all heard that comment, and we can read it in Hansard of Monday. Now he cannot say that he did not make that statement. It was made right in this House.
1 didn't say that industry, I said "an industry".

He stated that the industry in question that he was asked about had not modernized. The industry in question in my riding, the Texturon Mill in Hawkesbury, was only built in the mid-seventies. It is not a question of it modernizing. Had the Minister bothered to find out the facts before making his statements on Monday and today, he would not have got himself into the foot and mouth disease problem that he is in now.
I wish to read the letter sent to me by the industry in question. It states:
This letter is written objecting to the planned agreement on free trade with the U.S.A. You are familiar with our operation on Cameron Street in Hawkesbury at which we produce textured polyester yarn in a modern plant with excellent high speed equipment. Should total free trade with the U.S.A. be placed in effect, we beyond doubt will have to close our plant in Hawkesbury. We could not possibly compete with firms in the U.S.A., one of which presently produces in excess of 5 million pounds weekly. Our production in Hawkesbury is approximately 200,000 pounds weekly.
It is not an issue of modernization. The fact is that some of those plants in the United States could produce more in their coffee break than this plant in my riding produces in one week. That is the reality. There is over capacity in that plant. It can add a shift, or as I stated moments ago, cancel one break and it would be able to totally ruin and destroy an industry which provides the livelihood of 72 of my constituents. One would think that that being the case, the least that the Government could provide to my constituents is compassion and assistance instead of laughing at them and pretending that those industries deserve to be shut down, and presumably meaning that my constituents also deserve to be put out of work.
November 27, 1987

That is not good enough for the people whom I represent. Let me remind Members that whatever few votes there were for the Conservative Party in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell have gone with the rest of the votes throughout the rest of the country-out the window for the Tories.

The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell (Mr. Boudria) covered various areas in his speech, and I wish to touch on a few of them, one being the Alexandria subdivision. The Hon. Member mentioned certain letters received from Mr. Hanigan of VTA Rail, and also indications from CN as to its intention of continuing to provide service on this rail line between Montreal and Ottawa.
You have indicated, Mr. Speaker, that this is the rail line that you use, and a great many people share your concern. I also share the concern that this line continue to be in place in order that operations continue, as the management of VIA Rail and CN Rail intend. VIA Rail's indication was that almost indefinitely passenger service will continue to be provided between Montreal and Ottawa as it is a core service.
CN Rail has indicated that although the line is under review, as a great many lines are from time to time, to see that it is economically feasible to continue full operations, it does assure the people along that line who are using it for freight traffic that it will be continued for at least five years. That is all that it will guarantee any line of continued usage.
Most important is the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), who ultimately has the control in saying that this line will stay in place and continue to be available for Canadians, has indicated that without doubt this line will continue forever and ever. Although he does not put "forever and ever" in his statement, he certainly indicates that as long as he is around, which will be a long time, that that line will stay in place and continue to serve the people who use it, and who continue to want the services in that area.
Another point on the textile industry, Mr. Speaker, I too share the Hon. Member's concern as there are 3,000 constituents in my riding employed by Dominion Textile, which is the largest employer in my riding. Dominion Textile has three plants in my riding, one of which recently received a bronze award from the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion for productivity. I am very proud to stand here in the House and congratulate the employees and management of that company for their extraordinary effort, and perhaps setting an example for other people in the textile industry that they can compete and they will compete, given an opportunity.
This is where opportunity in our riding can be very important. Guaranteed access to the U.S. market is giving an opportunity for another plant of Dominion Textile to modernize and possibly expand. We look forward to a new way of life, and a new, grand market much larger than it is now for the Caldwell Mill in Iroquois. There are 400 people working at this plant, and I am sure that it will admit that its present operation is not as competitive as its operation to the south in
Supply
the United States. But the opportunity for this expanded market, guaranteed access to a market 10 times larger than the Canadian market, provides an opportunity for it to modernize and sell into that market aggressively.
Dominion Textile is no loser. It is presently aggressively expanding into the United States through acquisition and through continuing to force its way into that market and expand its market, and it will not change. That company will not change. It will continue on with guaranteed access to that market and will be able to supply products from Iroquois and the Long Sault plant to wherever it is able to market. Thank goodness for the free trade agreement because it will have guaranteed access to that market.

Mr. Speaker, I will respond briefly to those points. I thank the Hon. Member for his question. Unfortunately, as much as I respect my distinguished neighbour and colleague, I cannot agree with what he said.
First, he said that we have guaranteed access. I do not believe that that is so. A review done by Blake, Cassels & Graydon, a law firm which did a study for the Government of Ontario, refers to four criteria that were analysed in relation to the agreement. I read the operative paragraph of that report:
An application of these four criteria shows that the dispute settlement mechanisms contained in the Agreement are flawed in ways that are likely to result in a significant denial of Canadian access to the U.S. markets.
That is far from being guaranteed access in my opinion.
Second, in relation to the subdivision of CN Rail that both you and I, Mr. Speaker, think is very important, as does the Hon. Member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Warner), the Minister only gave his guarantee until 1992 and said that it would possibly be there longer than that. He said it would possibly be there much longer than that, to appropriately quote the Minister.
On April 20, 1987, the Save the Line Committee was totally dissatisfied with that answer and wrote a letter to the Editor of the Glengarry News under the heading: "Here we go again!" The first paragraph of the letter reads as follows:
First of all, I must take issue with your front page headline 'Alexandria rail line safe for five years, says Warner', which may give the uninformed reader the wrong impression. The line is anything but safe!
There is much more information in the letter which I do not have time to read now, but it was signed by Michael Cowley-Owen, the President of the Save the Line Committee of Alexandria. As Hon. Members can see, the information is not quite as it was reported a few moments ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Once again, Mr. Speaker, he spoke for 20 minutes about almost anything but the matter of transportation and particularly the deregulation of transportation under the Canada-United States free trade Agreement. Instead of reading a few comments, a few letters which he finds here and there, he would do better to consult with the industry at times, not only the various transportation industries but related industries as well.
Obviously, a free trade Agreement with the United States in the area of transportation is a necessary step. Let me explain. If we deregulate transportation in Canada, as the United States did before us, how could there be any fairness on both sides of the border without some trade agreement?
For instance, how could the trucking industry, particularly in Quebec, in Canada, compete with American transportation firms which have just been deregulated, which can get supplies of equipment, material, all kinds of items used for the maintenance of their truck fleet and so on, and which can buy goods to which no taxes or tariffs apply whereas the Canadian industry must carry that burden, Mr. Speaker.
Therefore, we must take these very important points in consideration in that free trade Agreement. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when we meet with some members of the industry, as I did myself a few weeks ago when I was in Los Angeles to meet with 200 transportation brokers of the Transportation Brokers Conference of America,

At the Transportation Brokers' Conference of America, 200 people directly involved in broking transportation in the trucking industry from Canada and the United States attended and asked very interesting questions. They are all very interested in getting an agreement on free trade between our two countries as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, the trucking industry is not the only one interested in the free trade deal. There is also, of course, the passenger service industry. There too the products are different. There cannot be adequate competition where an American or a Canadian business is involved because their products, their production costs and their equipment are different, and there cannot be legitimate and fair competition without a free trade deal in the passenger service sector.
The free trade deal will also bring a fundamental change in the transport industry in general; it will have an increasing
impact in the service industry, in manufacturing or tourism. That is extremely important, Mr. Speaker. There will be such an influx of or increase in traffic on both sides of the border that Canadian industries will benefit from a much more interesting potential volume of business than before. Mr. Speaker, this way, they will be even more competitive because our service industries have never been afraid of competition, but they will also be able to gain more customers, increase their potential and improve their services to the population.
Mr. Speaker, there is also a quite related . . .

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand the intervention of my colleague but I wish to mention the presence in the House of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) who has a lot of work to do within his party. There are not too many good Members left on the Liberal Party side, Mr. Speaker, and I understand that their Whip has a considerable amount of work to do. It is understandable that he may have to leave the House from time to time. Mr. Speaker, I firmly believe that the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) is, in fact, supporting the Government's position over the free trade deal with the United States.
I am also convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier is, like us, considering the importance of the free trade deal, particularly in the transportation industry, for the development of our manufacturing industries. Before Bills C-18 and C-19 and other regulatory measures, our manufacturing industries, particularly in remote areas, often were penalized as they had only access to a single carrier which could freely set its rates as it was the only one to hold a licence. It also could set the scheduling or the frequency of its service to that industry, which could prejudice its development.
Then, how could an industry, particularly in a remote area, become competitive not only with another industry in the same province, located in a large centre, in the same country, but also on the international market? Now, Bills C-18 and C-19
November 27, 1987

allow a carrier to find customers and to apply for a permit to the Department of Transport which will have to prove that this new carrier would prejudice the economy of the area or, on the contrary, assist the local industry. Once again, this relates perfectly with what might be considered now as a quasi-official free trade deal with the United States. The deregulation of transport allows Canadian industries to compete thanks not only to their productivity, or to the quality of their products, or to their marketing aggressiveness but also to their ability to get a better price, to move their goods at a better cost, which will allow them to become more competitive.
Deregulation, therefore, helps a business to become more competitive, and the Free Trade Agreement with the United States provides for an increase in its productivity.
Mr. Speaker, it is this Conservative Government, thanks to its leader the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), which has initiated this trade policy between Canada and the United States to effectively ... It is not always to harm Canadian men and women, Mr. Speaker, it is to help them develop and for the first time in the history of Canada, the only country with fewer than 100 million consumers ... we will have direct access to a market with over 100 million consumers, in fact with almost three times as much, over 250 million.
But what will over 250 million consumers do for our manufacturing companies? They will make it possible for them . . . They will provide them with a huge market which they did not have before. They will motivate them into creating better products, finding cheaper raw materials, as a result of the elimination of tariffs. They will be able to import cheaper raw materials. With greater volumes, they will be able again to increase their productivity, because Canadian men and women working in the manufacturing or processing industry are very aggressive and are not afraid to tackle a competitive market. They will be able to get it. They have already started and will continue to do so over the next few years, thanks to the Free-Trade Agreement with our American friends.
What is most important, besides the increased productivity and renewed aggressiveness of our companies is the fact that there was a shortcoming with regard to the ability to providing services, obtaining those products and delivering the goods whereas they were not competitive in the area of transport.
Now, with deregulation in Canada, our Canadian transportation companies and the American companies also, at the end of the line, will have better rates, more traffic, but with better rates, and at the end of the line, Mr. Speaker, who benefits the most if not consumers generally, and everyone in Canada? This is what the Prime Minister addressed in 1984 when he promised Canadians that we would restore the Canadian economy to a healthy state. This is what it means in my view, Mr. Speaker, giving the people, Canadians and Quebecers, a healthy economy. What does that mean? More subsidies. More social programs. When we can afford it, yes, Mr. Supply
Speaker, but it also means lower consumer prices, a larger range of products available to Canadians. Is that not economic health?
Mr. Speaker, transportation deregulation is extremely important. And when they talk about a sell-out, a sell-out of the transportation industry in order to get a free-trade agreement with the United States, they show total ignorance of the industry, Mr. Speaker.
Go and ask the President of CIL, and CIL I assume is also a Canadian company, and not a Toronto-only Canadian company at that. CIL, Canadian Industries Limited, Mr. Speaker, has facilities across Canada for manufacturing various goods. Ask those companies, like SICO Paint for instance, ask them what negative impact transportation deregulation has, and you will see how they will stress the positive aspects. Of course this is not a perfect system, but where on this planet, Mr. Speaker, can perfect systems be found? There may be perfect systems in the NDP lofty policies, but here we do not claim we have developed a perfect system of government management, Mr. Speaker. But we are very much aware of the importance of the manufacturing industry, of transportation, of those service industries. And all this is directly implied in the historic agreement which we are discussing, which the Premiers have been discussing yesterday in Toronto and will be discussing over the coming weeks.
Without this Free Trade Agreement, Mr. Speaker, Canada would remain a small country for us alone, maintaining the status quo which Opposition Members find so precious. But try to move a train when it is stopped on the track. It will not budge. Try to imagine what happens when you are moving ahead and decide all of a sudden to stop to maintain the status quo? You will very quickly realize that others are moving ahead, and you are standing still if you will have a somewhat reverse visual impact. You get the impression of moving backward when you are stopped. This is really the very short term effect of maintaining the status quo for a while: getting the impression that you are moving backward when everybody else is moving forward.
People are concerned about Canada's sovereignty in the Free Trade Agreement. Has Belgium, Holland, or Sweden, which is not even a member of the European Economic Community and which has a free trade agreement with that community, lost its sovereignty? Have the Swedes lost their language, have they lost their culture? Are the products imported by Sweden labelled exclusively in Italian, in Spanish, in German or in French? Yet, this is only a very small country of 10 million people next to a big giant, the European Economic Community which has a population of 300 millions. Have they lost their sovereignty for all that? Did these men and women lose pride in their Swedish citizenship? Of course not, Mr. Speaker. In no way have they lost anything. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker .. .

They did not give up anything either.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hear a new NDP Member say that they did not give up anything. Indeed, he should read what is being prepared and learn about the discussions that took place until now. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his comments the Hon. Member referred to my presence here and indicated I was in agreement with his suggestions. I would like to assure him that on the one hand I fail to share the views he has expressed, explained or developed. On the other hand, concerning the impact on the trucking industry in particular, I think he could have been modest enough to recognize that there is a problem in the Canadian and the American industries. The heart of the matter, in fact the heart of the dispute is that, according to the shipping industry, the wording indeed of the first annex and the later version may provide for easy access to Canada by American companies, at the expense of Canadian companies which were not given by this Government a firm commitment that we would have, loosely speaking, the kind of new, North American Jones Act that would allow Canadian companies, Canadian transportation workers to reach the American ports, to do on the American side what the current wording of the agreement allows Americans to do on our side here.
That is the heart of the problem, and the Hon. Member knows very well it is not accurate to state that the free trade agreement will have no impact on Canadian trucking. It will have an impact, a serious impact, and he knows it. I would ask him simply to be straight forward enough to admit it.
Let us look for a solution, let us try to amend the agreement. Indeed, this morning, there were reports through someone who knows about the issue, that the Mulroney-Reagan agreement, if there is to be one, may be amended one of the negotiators who stated today that yes, it is possible to bring in amendments. This is one amendment that will have to be made to the agreement, making sure it is fair and just for both sides.
The other question he raised in his conclusion, something I found quite interesting coming from him, is the so-called national pride.
I am asking him the question, because he knows that in Canada we have legislation or regulations providing that anything written on packaged or prepackaged products should
appear in both official languages, that is in French and English. Does he not agree with me that it would be advisable to include in the deal a safeguard for that Canadian legislation or those regulations which could be used by the Americans as a non-tariff barrier? Could they use that argument and say: "Listen now, in the United States we do not have two official languages. You are then setting an additional charge and it is unfair to impose Canadian bilingualism on the American manufacturing industry."
I say in all fairness that if it was possible to do it for security, as provided in the agreement, and for all kinds of things such as culture and marketing offices, then one of the most important legislation in the country, the one dealing with bilingualism, should be included.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will respond to the comments made by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (M. Gauthier). It is certain, first of all, that the trucking industry has an impact on free trade, and a very positive one at that, as I have said earlier.
Of course, I am no expert on transport, unlike the members opposite who all have so much to say on the subject. I have only been in the transport business for 20 years, in trucking as well as in passenger transport. So I do not at all consider myself an expert in the field, Mr. Speaker. However, the little I have learned, I do remember well.
I do not believe for a moment a problem exists between the United States and Canada. On the contrary. Deregulation and the free trade deal will be extremely beneficial to the transport industries, particularly those of Canada.
My time ran out before I could mention it earlier, but at the present time, in the passenger service sector, for instance, bus companies from Quebec or Canada, unless they have entirely defined routes, are not allowed on their way to Miami or Chicago or anywhere else to offer bus tours of New York or Washington when they go through those cities because they have no permit to do so and cannot get one either. It is the direct business, the one that is directly involved.
The same applies to Canada. Before deregulation, a group arriving in a smaller centre, in Quebec or in Canada, did not have anyone to handle its transportation needs and the carrier which had moved them from A to B could not do it either, because of the rules. Consequently, this is also, I believe, a significant improvement.
As to the national pride and the question of labelling, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) is right to raise that point, but it has already been discussed. The province and the Premier of Quebec would never have agreed to a Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement had the matter of labelling been questioned. Look at the number of countries presently doing business with the United States. A lot of goods manufactured in the United States are imported into Canada. There is certainly a lot of products manufactured in the United States and sold in Canada, and in Japan too.
November 27, 1987

Some Japanese-made products are sold in Canada bearing French labels and there is nothing in the Agreement . . . They have to do it for sure . . . Nothing in the Free Trade Agreement compromises ... It is covered and the Prime Minister was very clear at the onset. The Prime Minister of Canada has stated that social programs, marketing offices and culture were not to be touched.
Mr. Speaker, I would conclude on this because I would like to allow another member to put a question to me.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member spent some time defending the Government against what I believe are legitimate charges in the motion, that the rules imposed in this agreement will not be equal for Canadian airlines, ships, trucks and rail. They will not have the same access to the U.S. market as has been granted to those American transportation modes into Canada.
He talked about fear and how we had to get away from the status quo. I could not help but think of what was said some 300 years ago when doctors used to bleed patients. It became a common practice to bleed people, as this was considered a good practice to remain healthy. At the same time, some religious orders and others engaged in self flagellation. I believe we began to hear the same thing recently with respect to the economic field, with the saying of short term pain for long term gain. It sounds alarmingly like the same kind of methods are being practised on our economy and body politic.
Perhaps it is time to update our economic understanding and theories in this country, rather than to attack the status quo. The ancient doctors were quite convinced that anyone who had not been recently bled was unhealthy. I am wondering whether some of that same attitude has not gone into the political mindset in Canada, particularly when we rush into a proposed deal like this which clearly gives more benefits to the other party than ours in the field of transportation. The rationale is that while it will hurt in the short term, it will be good for the industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not as old as the Hon. Member to be able to comment on the ancient doctors. I have never been close to one and do not know their experience. Perhaps the Hon. Member does, but I am much too young.
As far as fear and the status quo is concerned, the Hon. Member has no trouble coping with the status quo of the Auto Pact. We know that the United Auto Workers are strong supporters of the NDP and they are quite content to be the only ones to have a free trade agreement with the United States.
When we talk about economic bodies, we are not only dealing with high level manufacturers. The first and most important economic body in Canada is consumers. It is Canadians, especially ordinary Canadians as the NDP like to
Supply
call them. We refer to them as strong and important Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join in the debate on this motion this afternoon which concerns two interrelated matters of Government policy.
First, I want to comment on the observations just made by the Parliamentary Secretary in relation to the comments of my friend, the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) who pointed out some of the dangers of free trade.
It may be useful to appreciate that the Auto Pact, which Government Members have often raised as an argument for the free trade deal which was negotiated this fall, is by no means a straightforward free trade agreement. It includes some very significant safeguards for Canadian content, continuing employment in Canada, and for a relationship between the number of cars sold in Canada and the production of automobiles in Canada. Those are the kinds of provisions that are very important to an agreement.
We had a free trade agreement in agricultural implements for many decades. That industry was forced to function in conditions under which prairie farmers and others were able to buy equipment made in the United States, without having to pay a duty. When we consider an industry such as that, the horrifying result is that there is precious little production by major producers in Canada.
We can use the example of the great company of Massey Harris as it was known years ago. The companies of Massey and Harris, were combined in the late nineteenth century in order to provide a stronger competitor for Canadian and export markets. This company, which later became Massey Ferguson, does very little production in Canada when we consider where the tractors and combines are made. The majority of its production for the Canadian market takes place in the United States.
While the farmer constituents in the riding of my friend for Humboldt-Lake Centre have benefited from free trade over the years, the results of free trade to the constituents of my friend, the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), where combines were made in the past, have meant the disappearance of that industry entirely.
To think that free trade is going to be some great panacea for the Canadian economy deserves very careful consideration, industry by industry. In that spirit, I would like to take up the motion before us this afternoon, "that this House condemn the

November 27, 1987
Supply
Government for its destructive influence on the Canadian transportation industry by its impractical and slavish adherence to the ideological myth of deregulation and its inept trade negotiations with the United States", and there are four paragraphs, and I would like to focus on two of those.
Paragraph 2 states:
(2) introduction in the railway industry of "Competitive Rail Line Rate" provisions allowing American railways free access to Canadian markets while denying reciprocal arrangements for Canadian railways;
And paragraph (4) states:
(4) abandoning its legislation on the Canadian coasting trade and failing to obtain any benefits in the trade agreement for Canadian maritime industries.
The Canadian railways provide us with a very interesting instance, again to use a specific example of an industry to focus the concerns we in the Opposition, particularly the New Democratic Party, feel about both the deregulation program and the agreement arrived at this fall. The railways, as 1 say, provide a fascinating case. Initially we find support for the program the Government was putting forward under its Freedom to Move rubric and in Bill C-18 and Bill C-19, in particular. There was very significant support from CP Rail and CNR for these provisions. When the railways looked more closely at what the Government was proposing to do, and when they focused on this competitive rail line rate provision, they suddenly did an about face.
Why did the railways, which have been so ideologically in line with the Government on its deregulation program, do that kind of about face? They discovered that what the Government was proposing on the Canadian side was a provision under which someone who had goods to ship could turn to the rail line and tell it that if it ships the goods to the border and ties in with an American line going to the vicinity of the market to which the individual wanted his goods shipped- using perhaps the Burlington Northern system across the West-and if the American railways quoted a significantly lower rate, the Canadian railway would be forced to use that particular system. The Canadian railway would not only be unable to quote the higher rate but would actually end up losing the income from carriage of those goods from the market, wherever it happened to be, perhaps in southern Ontario, to a western market.
When the Canadian railways realized that in the United States under its economies of scale, the massive amounts of freight the American railways carry, and under the much more favourable tax laws and the vicious labour laws which have operated there for the last years, this competitive rail line rate provision could threaten three-quarters of the trade the Canadian railways were doing, they did a most remarkable about face. I personally, as the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon, experienced that. Officials from the CP Rail office in Winnipeg arrived in my riding to have a chat with me.
In decades past, the tradition of the CCF and NDP, when officials of the CP Rail came calling, if they ever did, was to
have a very, very intensive encounter, indeed. In the mythology of our Party there is that moment when David Lewis said to a CP Rail president at a Rhodes Scholarship Committee, that if he were given the opportunity as Prime Minister of Canada, the first thing he would do would be to nationalize the CPR. That moment in the history of our Party stands in the sharpest contrast to what happened when these gentlemen arrived in my office in Thunder Bay. What they wanted to do was to have a close exchange of views in which they supported the criticism of my friend, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), of the Freedom to Move program and his criticism of what the Government is presuming to do with this deregulation program.
CP Rail became a supporter of our attack on deregulation. CP Rail, which is surely one of the remarkable fruits of enterprise in Canada-not necessarily competitive. There is a lot of monopoly about this business-recognized that what the Government was putting forward was a potential competition out of the United States which could well bring the railway to its knees, which could destroy the railway and employment in Canada, and make impossible the profitable state CP Rail has enjoyed, and which has made it such a producer of enterprise into other industries.
CP Rail enterprises have been the basis of much development in this country in the past, but the Government program of deregulation has every potential for destroying that for the future. There am I as a New Democrat making this odd speech in support of CP Rail at this point, but I am using it to demonstrate that the Government had the support of industry at one time, but after that industry considering the kind of concessions made to American interests on behalf of Canadian shippers, it no longer has that support. That has been mentioned by others.
Of course, Canadian shippers want to get the cheapest rate, but the Government thinks the only employment that counts in this country, the only prosperity that matters, is the production of minerals and chemicals. The Parliamentary Secretary alluded to CIL. Surely we want to ensure that the production of goods and their movement to markets in Canada and abroad are also productive of employment in transportation and communities.
In Thunder Bay, to focus on my own community again, where railway workers have been laid off in significant numbers by both CP Rail and the CNR, I see the proposals of the Government in its deregulation program as really destructive of employment and prosperity.
These proposals as they relate to the railways are reason enough for me to speak in support of the motion put forward this morning. What I would like to do now is to turn from the railways to the marine industries of this country, particularly to the shipbuilding industry. That is one with which I have been particularly concerned as critic in our caucus. I have had much reason to be concerned after conversations with shipyard workers and their managers, after visits to a variety of
November 27, 1987

shipyards from Vancouver to Halifax, and after meeting with shipyard workers here on the Hill. I can appreciate the plight of that industry.
This is another industry about which to put forward criticisms of the Government's actions, actions which underscore the critical attitude in general that has been taken. I might begin with a letter written by the president of the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association to the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) in the first days of this month. The letter was sent to a good number of cabinet Ministers and to all the Members of Parliament representing shipyards or related industries across the country. The letter states:
The purpose of this letter is to advise you of the preliminary views of the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association with respect to the document entitled "Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement-Elements of the Agreement". I say preliminary because this Association's Position will not be formalized until we have had an opportunity to study the completed document and its annexes, particularly the Transportation Annex.
He goes on to say:
In the interim, however, we would like you to be aware of our extreme dissatisfaction with the Agreement, insofar as it affects ship construction. You will undoubtedly recall that on December 8, 1986 the CSSRA announced publicly its full endorsement of a comprehensive bilateral trade agreement with the U.S.
This strong support assumed that the application of the U.S. Jones Act, the Burns-Tollefson Amendment, and other restrictive legislation concerning shipbuilding, on both sides, would be extended to cover both Canada and the U.S.
In other words, where the United States has restrictive legislation, or Canada might have some, including shipping interests and shipbuilders in the neighbouring country, those provisions would be spread so that the Americans would be able to take advantage of industries in Canada and Canadians could take advantage of activity in the United States.
That was the expectation. He goes on to state:
In our dialogue with the SAGIT on Marine, Industrial and Rail Equipment, we received encouraging reaction to this position. We believed at that time, and still do, that such a provision within a free trade agreement would be of mutual benefit commercially and militarily. However, to the extent that we can determine at this stage, just the opposite has occurred. The U.S. Jones Act (and its many amendments and revisions) are exempt from any provision of the Free Trade Agreement; the Agreement is silent with respect to the Burns-Tollefson Amendment; and no mention is made of the shipbuilding industrial sector on either side.
Thus we learned with some dismay that, apparently, our industrial sector was overlooked. Unfortunately, this does not surprise us, as the Government has been reluctant to consider the interests of Canadian shipyards with respect to national policy for many years.
When he says for many years he clearly recognizes that the failure of this Government to do anything for shipbuilding is a failure that characterized the preceding Liberal Government just as much.
The result of this is that the organization which has been renamed the Canadian Maritime Industries Association, formerly the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing
Supply
Association, put out a release with this letter declaring that the elements of the agreement that have been made public to date cause its members deep concern with respect to the construction of ships. The President in the covering release reiterates the hopes that they had of being able to benefit from American activity by having the restrictions of the Jones Act and other legislation removed. He said that instead the opposite appears to have occurred since the Jones Act governing ships engaged in U.S. domestic trade is specifically excluded from the free trade agreement. No mention is made of the shipbuilding industry.
That is reason enough for me as the critic for shipbuilding in our caucus to strongly support this particular motion. Here we have the failure of the Government to achieve anything in an agreement which members of the government party would declare is now the basic element in their strategy for Canada and their hopes for the prosperity of the country. Here is an industry that has been left out completely. What this reflects is the ongoing crisis of the shipbuilding industry to which I alluded earlier this afternoon in my statement under Standing Order 21.
We have the reality that the Party that now governs promised in August of 1984 to make shipbuilding a prosperous industry in Canada. That promise from members of the Atlantic caucus was surely a fairly considered decision since there were various items on which the Conservative Party promised action before it won election in September of 1984. In practice they have not done so. In practice there has been no action on these items. We have not had any statement of policy on shipbuilding at all.
Initially, people in the industry sought a statement. Eventually, they got to the desperate point of saying that if they had a policy statement saying that there is not going to be any policy even that would be something. What they have had to settle for is a policy which clearly accepts the decline of the industry, a policy that states, "We will assist you in rationalizing". In practice that means that the Government is saying, "Let's reduce the number of shipyards. Let's close them down".
This was most obvious when correspondence from Quebec came to the public eye early in 1985. That correspondence indicated that there was pressure being put on the yards on the St. Lawrence to have some of them put over completely to industrial work. The correspondence indicated that this was being accepted by the owner, by the Versatile interests, as justification for it to ask for more work and for more assistance from the Government for those yards that would continue in existence.
The ironic thing about this is that in the Province of Ontario yards have functioned over many years in St. Catharines, Collingwood and in my constituency at the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company. As the decline of traffic on the lakes hit these areas very severely in 1984, 1985 and 1986, and as the amount of repair work to be done declined, and as there was no building taking place at all, the bankruptcy of the

November 27, 1987
Supply
Government in the area of shipbuilding policy became a basis for companies to close their yards and to consolidate the remaining work.
Thus Collingwood, a yard at which fine commercial work had been done over many years, has disappeared. Never again will ships be built in that yard. What we have seen then and what we saw again this week with a demonstration yesterday of workers from Halifax who came to Ottawa to demonstrate against the Government to demand action on shipbuilding policy is a declaration that here is a government that may yield to political pressure. The next election draws near. We hear about a task force these days. The previous Government used the task force on deep sea shipping as a way to get past an election. This Government is thinking about a different kind of task force.
This Government has failed the shipbuilding industries completely. It is threatening shipping. It threatens the rail operations of the country. Here is a government that deserves the condemnation which this motion before us this afternoon states.

Mr. Speaker, when 1 hear my socialist colleague say that this Government has failed in the area of the shipping industry, of shipyards, etc., I suggest he is not aware of new developments. I think he should look around him and see what is going on across the country. Because Canadian Government orders in the area of defence are very significant in most Canadian shipyards, and if the Hon. Member had not been so subservient to the previous Government, today we would not have to make such an effort for capital expenditures in our defence system in order to buy boats, aircrafts, specialized trucks and so on.

Today I had some difficulty understanding exactly what was the message given in this House other than a series of specific criticisms. However, Mr. Speaker, I read today in this week's issue of the Financial Post, a newspaper that they probably never read because Mr. Bob White must subscribe to the Pravda and not to the Financial Post. The Hon. Member should go to the library once in a while where he could read the Financial Post for free. I also recommend that paper to the Liberal Members who have been criticizing since this morning during the debate on the motion by the Hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), who have been criticizing our deregulation policy and our free trade policy. So I was saying that in today's Financial Post one can read that the Canadian
Pacific, one of the biggest transport companies, has been taking measures in the past few months in order to be ready to tackle the enormous market that deregulation will open for development. And, Mr. Speaker, it says here and I agree, that by giving greater access to more carriers, by allowing negotiations between the carrier and users, this will result in a strong competition which in turn will lower the rates of transport. And when transportation costs are reduced . . . but Socialists are unaware of those things because they have never done any payroll work. They have always sponged on unions. When prices of goods are lowered in Canada as a result of reduced transportation costs, they become cheaper for all Canadians. This is what we do. We reduce consumer prices and thus extend our market abroad. However, you do not agree because you want to protect the free-trade situation that has prevailed in southern Ontario since 1965. Now it is impossible for Socialists to live with the requirements for competition and to have confidence in aggressive and glib Canadian industrialists who day after day are seeking new means of developing new and cheaper services for Canadians, because when everything is running smoothly in the system you sponge around and suck blood like leeches. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) has give me an opportunity to reiterate some points, and add one or two. I am grateful for that opportunity. As another Member who represents a shipbuilding area, the tone that he takes strikes me as a bit odd. When I was talking about railways, 1 don't think that he was paying any attention; he was paying as little attention as the Parliamentary Secretary who was packing up his papers and leaving as I made those comments. It would have been useful for him to stay and receive the education of some specific information instead of serving up rhetoric.
What we have received from this Government in the way of activity in the shipyards is no novelty. As it approached an election, the last Government served up a number of contracts to specific yards in order to keep them working. We got this "scrap" program as it was articulated, the special capital recovery program which saw ships built in various yards on government contracts for the Coast Guard and so on. The last Government knew that perfectly well, and this Government has been doing the same thing. As the election draws near, if enough government contracts go into the yards, people will be working.
What we did not have from the last Government, and have not had from this Government, despite the bluster that we were just served, is a declaration that the Government recognizes that by putting enough of those contracts into yards and changing certain provisions, such as the exemption from
November 27, 1987

duty of the largest fishing vessels so that they will not be imported but rather built here, it might be possible to keep work going in most of the yards of this country. We have not had that declaration as a policy, which it could be. Those who work in the yards, and those who own and manage them, would be very pleased to have the Government declare that as a policy.
Construction for Maritime Command was dreadfully neglected by the previous Government. By scheduling production for other services such as the Coast Guard, and determining the bases upon which the work will be distributed, there will not be those unseemly struggles between regions, for example with the St. Lawrence yard and the yard in the Hon. Member's riding working against the argument of the Saint John shipyard people that if the next six patrol frigates were built there, we will save $17 million a vessel-or is it on the whole package? We will not have those particular arguments being made. Those of us representing other yards, and Canadians generally will not be tempted to look through this thing and determine why Saint John Shipbuilding, which was a rather sorry starter, had reached the state of efficiency that might allow it to do that.
The Government has refused to state a policy, although it practises elements of it. It continues to argue that competitive bidding is actually the basis but does not look behind the bids-for example, the one that took the Simcoe to Marys-town-without considering the possibility that provincial government assistance is allowing a yard to underbid other yards. People have not been getting into those questions, at least in public, whatever may happen in Transport Canada. There has been a failure to state a policy, and then the Hon. Member has the gall to rise and bluster at me.
Bill C-52 relates to the coasting trade of the country and it might offer something or other, but it is an odd situation. The Bill has been given second reading in the House. I understand the legislative committee is on hold. Is it on hold until after the trade deal is passed in order that we avoid disrupting anything, or why is it that this particular Bill not being acted upon?
If one looks carefully at Bill C-52 and the exemptions within it, one of the most harmful exemptions is for platforms used in the production of hydrocarbons. Those platforms out there are involved in drilling and production, particularly off the Atlantic coast, and they are ships of a sort. They could be built in Canadian yards. This Government has given us legislation that will allow import of them rather than construction in Canadian yards; not that they will be licensed, but they are simply exempted entirely from the Bill. What type of policy is that?

Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to have an opportunity to participate in this debate today. The whole question of transportation is extremely important to the West, and that was the perspective I wished to bring to the debate. It is demonstrated by the fact that over 50 per cent of our exports to the United States are handled by trucking; 75 per cent of
Supply
the imports to Canada are handled by trucking. Already we are seeing Canadian companies competing quite effectively in the United States.
I wish to go into that issue in a lot more detail, but obviously the time is not available.
The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) has western roots, and he was born in the West. As I grew up in the West, there were two things that were particularly aggravating to western Canadians. The first one has always been the high cost of shipping, and the second has been the high tariffs which we have seen as an intrusion to western Canadians rather than an assistance. We have always seen those items as a problem rather than a solution. What I see happening in this motion before us today is a combination of both free trade and transportation.
Will the Hon. Member address for a moment the impact that this has had on western Canada? Surely he would agree with me that through Bills C-18 and C-19 the western Canadian shipper, who has for years been at a disadvantage, as a result of Bills C-18 and C-19 is today moving into a position of advantage and opportunity, which we see as a big chance in the West. The free trade agreement will remove those tariffs which historically have been a real hindrance and burr in the saddle of western Canadians.
Perhaps the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) could condense his answer to approximately 60 seconds.

If I only have 60 seconds, I will not address the tariffs.
As someone who grew up on a mixed farm in Manitoba with a father who sold grain through Thunder Bay and used the Seaway, I have a very great interest in western shipping and in using rail lines out of the West. We ought to recognize the importance of those lines.

My predecessors in the last Parliament who fought for the Crow Rate wanted to maintain low rates. They did not want any deregulation-style arguments or competitive enterprise arguments to be used to reduce this particular rate. The railways have been able to manage. Some subsidies were provided to them. A subsidy that is now under attack had been provided in order to maintain that.
I am sure that you wish me to stop, Mr. Speaker, but let me put forward those items. The Hon. Member's comments seem to be quite consistent with my position, which is at variance with the people who put forward this motion, and the position taken in the last Parliament. I am not sure it is in keeping with

what the Hon. Member wants. I feel that he ought to reconsider his own position more firmly in terms of the Crow Rate in particular.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that another Member wishes to say a few words before the debate concludes, so I will try to be as brief as possible.
This particular motion talks about "inept trade negotiations" that the Government has with the United States. The mover of the motion used the word "inept". According to the Oxford Dictionary "inept" means "out of place", so we can say the out of place trade negotiations; "inept" also means "absurd", so we could say the absurd trade negotiations. It also means "silly", so we could say the silly trade negotiations. It also means unskillful.
Most of the speakers who have addressed the resolution today have mentioned in the areas of airlines, railways, and trucking and that the Government of Canada has been inept in dealing with the United States. According to what has been placed on the record today about that entire group of subjects, one could say that the principle of free trade as the Government sees it is inept.
When members of the public are asked what free trade means, they think that free trade means free trade, that countries can trade freely without having any obstacles like tariffs placed in their paths at the border and that products can move freely across two borders, three borders, five borders or 10 borders. That is the way some trade agreements operate. We say that this is an inept pact because there is no free trade deal. The free trade deal with the United States does not provide for free trade.
Today, the Premier of Newfoundland must have eaten something bad or he must not have got enough sleep last night. This afternoon he said that he was in agreement with the free trade deal with the United States. I do not know what came over him.
Under this free trade agreement, a producer in Puerto Rico could say that the Government of Newfoundland has put a subsidy on a product by bailing out a company in Newfoundland and therefore he wants a duty placed on that product when it enters the United States market. Under the so-called free trade agreement with the United States, one producer in the United States of America, even the owner of a corner store if he produces something, has the right to ask for such a duty to be placed against products from Canada.
Countervailing tariffs and anti-dumping legislation are all fancy terms which only mean that a charge, whether it be a tariff, a duty, a countervailing duty or an anti-dumping duty, must be put up when products cross the border. I do not care what it is called, it is all money. This happens when one
country believes that another country is bringing products across the border unfairly.
We are saying in this motion that Canada was inept because Canada agreed to abide by U.S. law. Some Hon. Members have said that this will remove tariffs at the border and therefore it is a great thing because now we can move our goods across the border without having that encumbrance of a tariff.
What does a producer in the United States do when computing a countervailing duty? The producer claims that he has been damaged by Canadian subsidies and the total damage is assessed. The American Department of Commerce sends representatives to Canada and, by mutual agreement, goes over the books of the company concerned and holds a hearing at which the company concerned can claim that there is no subsidy or the Government can claim that the American producer is wrong. The total value of the claimed subsidy is taken into account.
Under the free trade agreement, the United States can still say that because Canada is different from the United States, it will impose tariffs. In fact, Canada is vastly different from the United States. Our social programs are vastly different and many people would praise that difference.
There is a big difference between getting sick in Canada and getting sick in the United States. There is a big difference between ending up in hospital in Canada and ending up in hospital in the United States. The difference is absolutely incredible. In Canada, there is social legislation and legislation to help industry. In fact, there are special government Departments in the poorer provinces of Canada that give tax breaks and special DR1E assistance.
Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, the north shore of Quebec and northern Ontario all have access to assistance programs for industry. The Government gives interest-free loans to companies to set up industries in those areas or its gives half loans and half grants to industries to expand tourist facilities and hotels. All of these things assist the poorer regions in Canada, and these are programs that do not exist in the United States.
The United States does not offer assistance to fishermen who own boats. There are no plant-modernization programs for the forest industry in the United States. However, we have such programs in Canada.
The free trade agreement will now become the primary target of this great protectionist attitude in the United States. Producers are blaming their problems on cheap imports. These producers know that the United States has told Canada to sign on the dotted line so that Canada will respect American trade laws, anti-dumping laws and countervailing duty laws. Canada has signed on the dotted line. Canada said: "Yes, for the first time in history, we will sign on the dotted line that says we respect your right to impose a countervailing duty on a product that comes from Canada that you believe has been subsidized
November 27, 1987

by the Government of Canada or by a provincial Government".
That is why I cannot understand the Premier of Newfoundland. In fact, understanding what is in the free trade agreement, I wonder why any premier from any Atlantic province would agree to such a stupid deal, a deal that means that we no longer believe in assisting the poorer regions with special government assistance or programs.
Recently, the Premier of Newfoundland and his Cabinet decided to give millions and millions of dollars in loans to a company from Alberta so that it would move to Mount Pearl outside St. John's, Newfoundland, to grow cucumbers. I do not know whether it was $11 million, $12 million or $13 million which was given to this company to grow cucumbers. That provides a good opportunity for a countervail. We will see what happens when that company tries to export those cucumbers to the United States if they can grow them. There is no government assistance in the United States comparable to that kind of assistance. That is what the Premier of Newfoundland did, but today he has said that he agrees with the free trade agreement into which this Government has entered. Why, 1 do not know. What other deal was made behind the scenes? Maybe there was another deal made, I do not know.
The Hon. Member who moved the motion is saying that the Government of Canada went to the United States and said that it would sign a free trade deal with the United States that would provide that Canada respects all the American laws and rights to impose duties. Canada has signed an agreement saying that it will respect American state trucking laws and the right of the United States to impose a charge on a product that comes into the United States if a producer in the United States so wishes. That is why we call it inept and all of those words to which I referred in the Oxford Dictionary, particularly the word "silly".
I have never heard anything more silly than calling this a free trade deal. Charges can still be made under GATT. Countervailing duties can be applied. Anti-dumping laws and duties can be imposed when any U.S. producer wishes. So why is it called a free trade deal? Because the Government says it will remove tariffs. Yet it does not go on and explain that countervailing duties could be double the old tariff. In other words, countervailing duties of 20 per cent were applied to saltfish, which has a normal tariff of 10 per cent. That countervailing duty would have been 30 per cent if the tariff was not in place because the damage being done to the U.S. producers was judged to be 35 per cent of the value of the product in Canada. That is basically why we disagree with the free trade deal.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my colleague for giving me a few minutes to make some comments on this Opposition motion dealing with the deregulation of the transportation industry and the free-trade deal.
I think that by criticizing this historic free-trade deal, the Opposition lacks preparation and respect. The simple cooperation of the Liberal opposition with the socialists makes us wonder if the Liberals are opposed to free-trade because they are seeking electoral gains or if they are trying to protect the interests of some regions of the country to the detriment of the others.
In any event, I think that when the Opposition agrees with Bob White, who is the boss of the socialists in this Camber, it lacks respect for Canadians in general and particularly for Canadian businessmen, entrepreneurs and industrialists who export to the U.S. goods and services worth $95 billion, out of our total exports of $125 billion. These are the Canadians whose aggressiveness and capacities developed the U.S. market. These are the Canadians who are attacked by the Opposition today, in this Chamber. What the Opposition is saying is that we must prevent our Canadian exporters from getting access to the U.S. market. This is what they are telling us by attacking free-trade.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: This is absolutely false.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
They refuse to recognize that free-trade exists in Canada, in Southern Ontario, since 1965 in the auto industry. It was the same negotiator, Mr. Reisman, who negotiated the Auto Pact that proved to be very beneficial. These same socialists and their leader of the time, Mr. Douglas, were against free trade. But today, they would like to keep the benefits of free trade for the automobile industry only. They do not want to see similar benefits extended to all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, we should realize that that first free trade initiative in 1965 results today in sales of $33 billion a year for Canadian exporters and 840,000 jobs in the automobile industry. And we have here people who oppose a more national implementation of free trade. I wonder how serious they can be and where is their respect for all Canadians. I wonder where is their respect for the 12 million Canadians, out of a population of 20 million, who have a job and are productive.
Older people do not work, of course, and neither do the young and the sick and those unable to work. But the 12 million Canadians who do work have a production of $500 billion worth of goods and services in Canada. One quarter of that is exported. That means that there are 3 million Canadian men and women who have jobs today because of our exports. And people opposite have the gall to pick on details in the trade deal.

Mr, Speaker, it is important that Canadians understand that we initiated and concluded the deal first of all to secure our continued access to the American market. The fact is that the Americans also have problems and are increasingly being pressured by the business people because of their substantial trade deficit. Recently, they have had a yearly trade deficit of $170 billion. This has an impact on all American companies, whatever their size. This has brought about protectionism and congressional pressure. The congressmen are preparing bills to eliminate and reduce the import of certain products, and as far as we are concerned, the products most affected are those sold by our Canadian business people, whose hability has naturally been questioned by the socialists, and also by the Liberals to gain the favour of the voting public.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask the opposition to stop making negative statements about this historic Free Trade Agreement. I even ask them to support us, because if the socialists and the Liberals opposite go on sleeping together in the big Bob White Hotel, it will mean the end of this country, as they are now concentrating in the central region of this country all the benefits of free trade and telling the rest of Canadians that free trade is bad. As for the Quebec Liberal Members in this House, they are not even able to understand the message of Quebecers as a whole, of the Quebec government and of premier Bourassa, who are all saying that free trade is good and even essential for Quebec. The Liberals prefer to bow down before those who defend the interests of Southern Ontario. Mr. Speaker, I believe that they should also think
about what is good for Quebecers and all Canadians. That is my message for them. Thank you.
